10108-a-treatise-of-daunses-wherin-it-is:
Printed in 1581, this short Puritan tract argues that dancing leads Christians toward sexual sin and should have no place in godly life. Its author writes in the plain, stern voice of the English reform movement, quoting Scripture and warning readers not to treat the question as small. Plays come under the same attack, joined to dance as a linked moral danger.

The tract answers mockers who laugh at the subject and readers who think larger church questions matter more. It builds its case step by step, tying steps, music, and mixed company to lust and to loss of self-control. Readers get a clear window into early Puritan fears about pleasure, the body, and public show.
10266-the-glands-regulating-personality-:
Louis Berman, a Columbia physician, published this popular science book in 1922, arguing that glands of internal secretion shape human nature. Berman treats the thyroid, pituitary, adrenals, gonads, and thymus as an interlocking directorate that guides body and mind. The book helped bring endocrinology to a wide public.

Chapters trace how glands were found, how they steer growth, sex, and mood, and how they may explain types of personality and historic figures. Berman ends with uses and hopes for the future. Readers get a bold, early survey of hormones, dated in parts, but lively and clear.
10389-northern-trails-book-i:
William J. Long published this first book of Northern Trails in 1905, as book six of his Wood Folk series. Long, a popular nature writer, tells animal lives as stories, with wolves, trails, and snow as his stage. A glossary of Indian names helps young readers follow the woodland terms.

Wayeeses the strong one, the old wolf's challenge, and trails that cross in snow form the core tales. A white wolf hunts, mothers guard young, and death watches in silence. Readers get vivid, old-style nature stories, best read as fables of the wild rather than strict science.
10920-two-years-ago-volume-i:
Charles Kingsley's novel opens with two friends visiting Whitbury in Berkshire, looking back on a crisis two years earlier. One of them, Claude Mellot, a witty London art lover, recalls a time of pestilence and war, when there was work to do and little time to reflect. The story then rewinds to those crowded months and the people caught in them.

Volume one introduces a Berkshire village cast: doctors, squires, and sharp-tongued neighbours such as Miss Heale, whose schemes and grudges stir trouble. Kingsley mixes social comedy with earnest questions about duty, faith, and class. Readers meet a Victorian England of parish life, gossip, and moral argument, told with energy and a preacher's eye for character.
11054-poems-1786-volume-i:
Helen Maria Williams published this first volume of poems in 1786, dedicated to the Queen. Williams apologises for a confined education and youth, noting that her first poem, the legendary tale of Edwin and Eltruda, was written to amuse solitary hours and published on Dr. Kippis's advice. Favourable reception encouraged her to publish an Ode on the Peace and a poem called Peru, revised for this collection.

Other poems, new to print, show a young writer's humility before powerful patrons and partial friends. Williams writes with feeling about friendship, nature, and history, in the polite verse of her day. The volume gives readers an early work by a writer who later became known for French Revolution writings, and it shows her beginnings as a poet.
11546-the-autobiography-of-a-journalist-:
William James Stillman's first volume, published in 1901, traces a New England boyhood shaped by his mother, early nature worship, and religious feeling, then an American education and college life. Art study in America and England follows, with a mission for Kossuth and student days in Paris.

Later chapters cover spiritism, life in the wilderness, and the turn to journalism, with Cambridge, the Adirondack Club, Emerson, and Agassiz along the way. The volume closes with his Roman consulate, and it reads as both memoir and a record of American art and letters.
12031-collected-poems-1901-1918-in-two-v:
Walter de la Mare's Collected Poems 1901 to 1918, volume 1, published in 1920, gathers his early lyrical work. Contents list Poems of 1906, including Shadow, Unregarding, They Told Me, Sorcery, The Children of Stare, Age, The Glimpse, Remembrance. Treachery in Vain, with The Miracle, Keep Innocency, and The Phantom Voices.

Later poems include Thule, The Birthnight, The Death-Dream, Where Is Thy Victory, Foreboding, Vain Finding, Napoleon, England, Truce, Evening, Night, and The Universe. Volume 1 shows de la Mare before the children's songs of volume 2: a poet of shadows, dreams. Quiet terror, whose lyrics made the unseen feel close at hand.
12073-letters-of-horace-walpole-volume-i:
Charles Duke Yonge selected and edited this first volume of Horace Walpole letters, published in 1890. Walpole, son of prime minister Robert Walpole, wrote to friends for over fifty years, and his letters became a running chronicle of English society.

This volume covers 1736 to 1764, from schoolboy notes to Montagu through the Grand Tour, Paris salons, Versailles, and London politics. Walpole reports marriages, duels, plays, elections, and gossip with wit and sharp eyes for fashion and folly. The letters also show a collector and antiquary forming his tastes. Together they give an intimate view of eighteenth-century elite life, told by one of its keenest watchers.
12434-twelve-studies-on-the-making-of-a-:
Charles Foster Kent and Jeremiah Whipple Jenks wrote these twelve studies on the beginnings of Israel's history, as part of a series on the Bible's message to modern life. The volume opens with Garibaldi's praise of the Bible as an ally of freedom. Choate adds that American schools, industry and liberty owe much to emigrants who landed with the English Bible in hand.

Studies move through Israel's early story, from patriarchs and exodus toward nationhood, drawing moral and civic lessons for modern readers. Kent and Jenks write for study groups, with questions and clear narrative. The book shows early twentieth-century Bible teaching at work, joining scholarship to citizenship in a hopeful, progressive key.
12649-analyzing-character-the-new-scienc:
Katherine M. H. Blackford and Arthur Newcomb's 1922 Analyzing Character, the new science of judging men, treats misfits in business, home and social life. Contents cover causes of misfits, elements of fitness, classes of misfits, and the physically frail. The fat man, the man of bone and muscle, slaves of machinery, the impractical man, hunger for fame and waste of talent in professions follow.

Vocational guidance, in this system, reads body, face and habit to place workers rightly. Blackford, a physician, writes with early twentieth-century confidence in character science. The book now reads as a period document, revealing how employers once sorted people, and how psychology, physiology and prejudice mixed in the search for fit workers.
12652-george-washington-volume-i:
Henry Cabot Lodge's first volume on George Washington, standard library edition 1889, covers youth, planter life and the road to command, closing with peace and an index. Illustrations show Washington from Stuart's Athenæum portrait, an autograph from a bill of exchange, the home of the Washington family, Lawrence Washington from an Alexandria painting, and Miss Mary Cary.

Lodge, a statesman-historian, presents Washington's character formed by family, land and duty, before the presidency treated in volume two. The volume offers a classic, admiring life, written for general readers who wanted the founder's early years in full. Its illustrations, from Stuart and family portraits, give the text a visual anchor.
12800-abraham-lincoln-volume-i:
John T. Morse Jr.'s 1899 biography, first of two volumes, traces Abraham Lincoln from his rough Illinois youth to the early Civil War. Chapters cover his start in life, law and Congress, the debates with Stephen Douglas, election, and the first acts of war. A portrait and a Gettysburg Address facsimile enrich the edition.

Morse treats Lincoln as a political mind formed by prairie life and courtroom argument, not as a saint. The Lincoln-Douglas debates get full weight, since slavery's spread forced the nation's choice. The volume ends with Lincoln learning, under fire, how to be a war president in fact.
12918-iranian-influence-on-moslem-litera:
M. Inostranzev's Iranian Influence on Moslem Literature, part one, translated from Russian by G. K. Nariman in 1918, traces Persian roots in Arabic letters. Chapters cover Arabic writers as sources for Sasanian culture, Parsi clergy preserving tradition, ethico-didactic books of Iranian origin, Arabic adab literature, and Pahlavi books studied by Arab authors. Appendices add Zoroastrian princes and the trial of Afshin.

A chapter on Ali ibn Ubayd ar Rayhani, reputed author of a Persian-titled adab book, shows how Persian matter reached Arabic readers. Inostranzev writes for scholars of comparative literature. The study remains a solid early work on Persian-Arab cultural transfer.
13011-far-off-or-asia-and-australia-desc:
Far Off, published in New York in 1852 by the author of The Peep of Day, describes Asia and Australia for young readers through anecdotes and pictures. Its frontispiece shows an English lady teaching Jewish and Muslim girls near Jerusalem, listening as a child of eight speaks of Jesus as redeemer. The book's aim is plain: to teach geography through stories a child can hold.

Chapters move country by country, from China, where a boy offers his own skin to flies to spare his parents, to Burma, where making idols and pagodas counts as great goodness. The author explains pagodas, idols, and rebirth in simple terms, always with a missionary moral close at hand. Modern readers will note its dated views, but its method, story first and fact second, is clear throughout.
13105-memoirs-of-margaret-fuller-ossoli-:
Volume one of the memoirs of Margaret Fuller Ossoli, published at Boston in 1857, gathers friends' memories, letters, and early writings about a leading American thinker. Fuller was known for wide learning, sharp talk, and a gift for drawing out others. The volume opens with her youth and her circle, and quotes those who knew her best.

Friends recall her frank ease with girls her own age, her lack of jealousy, and her joy in company. One passage marvels at a woman who seemed to know all languages and who read a friend's life at will. The memoir is less a straight life than a portrait built from many voices, and it shows why Fuller stirred both praise and puzzlement in her time.
13223-poems-by-jean-ingelow-in-two-volum:
Volume one of Jean Ingelow's Poems, Boston 1896, author's complete edition, is dedicated by the poet to her brother George Kilgour Ingelow from Kensington in June 1863. Contents run from Divided Honors and Requiescat in Pace to Supper at the Mill, Scholar and Carpenter, The High Tide on the Coast of Lincolnshire, and Songs of Seven. Ingelow writes in a clear, musical voice.

One poem hears service bells far off, a freshet springing from moss, bluebells leaning across, and bees murmuring in milk-white bloom. Another tells a dreamer visited by Remorse, who wakes, vows to repair wrongs, be just and kind, and amend his ways. The volume shows Ingelow at her best: tender, moral, and full of English country feeling.
13496-the-white-morning-a-novel-of-the-p:
Gertrude Atherton's The White Morning, a novel of German women in wartime, opens in Munich at long dusk, where. Countess Gisela Niebuhr stares over the Englischer Garten and recalls the causes of her dissatisfaction with her country as a woman. Thoroughly disgusted as a German, she prepares for a momentous role with the dawn.

Gisela remembers girlhood from fourteen, her sister, and Heloise von Erkel, the most tragic figure in Munich, faded in hair and complexion yet distinct in bearing. Talk of Social Democrats overturning the Hohenzollerns and stretching out a young republic's hand meets the cry of death to the last man rather than defeat. Atherton imagines women, not armies, breaking a nation's war.
13613-studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-v:
Havelock Ellis's fourth study in the psychology of sex, Sexual Selection in Man, treats touch, smell, hearing, and vision as senses in attraction. The 1927 preface warns that the work is tentative and preliminary, mapping a field in broad outlines before knowledge constellates into measurable shapes.

Ellis notes that writers on love, from Sénancour and Stendhal to Michelet, often passed over smell as too unaesthetic, while poets mentioned odours more than novelists did. A Mainz chronicle of 1367 shows men's tunics made so that the body could be seen in walking or sitting, a rare insistence on naked display. The volume gathers history, physiology, and literature into a study of how senses shape desire.
14031-the-colloquies-of-erasmus-volume-i:
Desiderius Erasmus's Colloquies appear here in N. Bailey's translation, edited by E. Johnson in 1878. Volume one gathers dialogues on courtesy in saluting, family discourse, rash vows, and benefice-hunters. A soldier's life, a master's commands, and a schoolmaster's admonitions follow. Plays, child's piety, hunting, and scholastic studies add variety.

Later colloquies treat profane feasts, religious treats, lovers, and uneasy wives. A forged letter episode shows bishops tricked by a false confession about translating the Old Testament. Erasmus uses talk to satirise clergy, schools, and manners. The dialogues suit students of Renaissance humanism. Bailey's English keeps their wit and bite.
14238-frank-reynolds-r-i:
A. E. Johnson's volume in the Brush, Pen, and Pencil series presents Frank Reynolds with forty-six examples of his work. Publishers argue that black-and-white press art deserves permanent form, since most of it vanishes with the daily paper. Reynolds, trained at Heatherley's under Professor John Crompton, learned drawing as the dominant note, with a sure hand and unerring instinct.

Press comedy made his name. Armed with a sharp pencil and sharper humor, Reynolds drew regularly for the illustrated press, joining the clever band at Pick-Me-Up in its sunniest, most audacious days. One plate shows Georgette at the Moulin Rouge: thin-lipped, pale as ivory, motionless until song lights her face from within. Comedy nears tragedy here, Johnson notes, and Reynolds strikes both with equal truth. Art lovers meet a draftsman of life's little comedies at his best.
14360-the-dawn-and-the-day-or-the-buddha:
Henry T. Niles wrote this long verse narrative, published in Toledo in 1894, as the first part of a comparison of the Buddha and Christ in poetry. The opening books follow Prince Siddhartha from palace life toward renunciation.

Niles retells court scenes, marriage, dreams, and the prince's encounters with age, sickness, and death in flowing blank verse. He frames both teachers as bringers of light to a suffering world, while keeping their stories distinct. The poem is devotional and earnest, a nineteenth-century American attempt to set Eastern and Christian teaching side by side.
14748-for-the-faith-a-story-of-the-young:
Evelyn Everett-Green sets this historical novel among young reformers at Oxford in the early Reformation years. Its heroes are students and townsmen drawn to new ideas about faith, scripture and church reform, and willing to argue for them at personal risk.

Chapters follow friendship, love and danger as the group faces governors, prison and harsh treatment. Some accept reconciliation; others hold firm. John Clarke and Henry Sumner are named among those who died from the effects of imprisonment, unabsolved. Notes at the end admit where histories disagree, grounding a stirring tale in a disputed but real episode.
15272-spenser-s-the-faerie-queene-book-i:
George Armstrong Wauchop edited Spenser's Faerie Queene, Book One, with introduction and notes, in a Macmillan edition first set up in 1903 and reissued in 1921. The introduction covers the age that made the poem, Spenser's life, romantic epic form, new learning, allegory, stanza, and diction. A letter to Raleigh fronts the text.

Book One follows the Red Cross Knight through twelve cantos, with notes and glossary to aid students. Wauchop's edition suits college readers new to Spenser. Fans of Renaissance poetry will find the volume a clear, scholarly gateway to a great, if demanding, epic.
15519-representative-plays-by-american-d:
Oliver Bell Bunce's Love in '76, an incident of the Revolution, appears here as part of a collection of representative plays by American dramatists, 1856 to 1911. An introduction notes that Bunce's name is little linked to the American theatre, yet his comedietta is a satisfactory example of parlor comedy, sprightly and freshly inventive.

The play premiered at Laura Keene's Theatre in New York on February 28, 1857, for the benefit of the Shirt Sewers' Union, second on a double bill with Faust and Marguerite. Laura Keene, Stoddart, Ringgold, and J. G. Burnett acted in it. Critics of the day called it a nice little play, though they balked at the word comedietta. The piece invites comparison with Royall Tyler's The Contrast, in manner and spirit.
1676-alcibiades-i:
Plato's Alcibiades I, translated by Benjamin Jowett and possibly spurious, opens with Socrates addressing the ambitious young Alcibiades, who dreams of ruling Athens and the world. Socrates warns him that he lacks self-knowledge, and that power without knowledge of the good is mere flattery of the crowd.

Through questions on justice, the useful, and the self, the dialogue urges Alcibiades to know himself before he leads others. An appendix on the Platonic canon frames the text. The work is a fine introduction to Socratic education, whether Plato's own or a follower's.
16793-the-river-and-i:
John G. Neihardt wrote this tale of a youthful river trip, first as a serial in Putnam's Magazine in 1909 and as a book in 1910, here in a 1927 Macmillan new edition. It came five years before his Song of Hugh Glass, first piece of his Western Cycle. The note says the tale was written in the winter of 1908.

Neihardt tells of camp nights, river miles, and young daring on a western stream, with pictures to match. The voice is that of a poet looking back at his own green years. Readers who love river tales and western verse will find a warm, early Neihardt, full of water, sky, and the pull of a long trip downstream.
16805-the-jungle-fugitives-a-tale-of-lif:
Edward S. Ellis wrote this 1903 book of Indian adventure plus many American tales, issued by Hurst in New York. The title tale opens in spring 1857, as rumblings of uprising spread through India and plotters pass from end to end of the empire. Other tales run from lost in the woods and lost in the South Sea, through cyclones, blizzards, riatas, and waterspouts, to a heroic woman and a battle in the air.

Ellis writes for boys in brisk, plot-first style, with danger, escape, and daring in each short tale. The Indian tale reflects its age's views of empire, which modern readers will read with care. As period adventure, the book offers fast, vivid stories of flight and survival on land and sea.
17017-the-life-and-letters-of-walter-h-p:
Burton J. Hendrick's first volume of Walter H. Page's life and letters follows the North Carolina boy from Reconstruction youth to journalism, then to London as ambassador. Chapters cover the forgotten man, the Wilson era, England before the war, Mexico, Panama, and the fight to keep America out of the European war. Letters and papers fill out the tale.

Hendrick drew on Page's papers, on talks with Viscount Grey, and on British Foreign Office files. The result is a rich, detailed life of a diplomat at a turning point. Readers keen on Anglo-American ties and the road to 1917 will find this volume a deep, well-sourced start to the story.
17514-the-garden-you-and-i:
Barbara, author of The Garden of a Commuter's Wife, published this garden book with Macmillan in New York and London in June 1906. The contents move from the ways of the wind and the book of the garden, you, and I. They pass through hardy plants, a garden vacation, and annuals worthy and unworthy. Then come a fortunate escape, a simple rose garden, a midnight adventure, and ferns, fences, and white birches.

Readers get a garden book written as a friendly talk, mixing practical notes on plants with stories of garden life. The author's voice is chatty and personal, treating the reader as a fellow gardener. It suits gardeners who like their advice wrapped in anecdote, and readers of Edwardian domestic writing.
17811-grace-harlowe-s-junior-year-at-hig:
Jessie Graham Flower wrote Grace Harlowe's Junior Year at High School in 1911, the third book in the High School Girls series, printed in Philadelphia by Altemus. Grace, a bright, loyal schoolgirl, now faces the pull of sororities and the test of fast friends.

Chapters bring a new arrival, confidences, an autumn walk, a discovery, and the Phi Sigma Tau, with Eleanor throwing down a challenge and a rescue party to close the term. Flower writes clean, cheerful school tales of pluck, sport, and loyal chums. Girls who liked school stories of the day will still enjoy Grace and her set.
18077-we-and-the-world-a-book-for-boys-p:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote We and the World, a book for boys, part one, printed for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London and New York. Ewing dedicates the book to her twelve nephews, by name, from the Smiths to the Gattys.

The book opens on English landscape, calm and settled, with home-bred virtues and local ties that speak for the moral character of the land. Boys' tales of home, school, and the world follow, in Ewing's warm, moral style. It is a gentle Victorian boys' book, full of English country life and the duties of young gentlemen.
18213-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
Volume three of The Story of the Great War covers the war begins, the invasion of Belgium, and the battle of the Marne. The volume opens with King George V and King Albert inspecting Belgian troops, with the Prince of Wales close by.

Part one runs from the attack on Belgium and the siege of Liège to Louvain, Brussels, Mons, Charleroi, and the great retreat. The Marne chapters then trace Allied and German plans, first moves, and the German retreat. The book is a clear, period history of 1914's opening months, rich in maps, pictures, and battle detail.
18217-chambers-s-elementary-science-read:
Chambers published this first book of elementary science readers, with object lessons and illustrations, for Standard One pupils. The London and Edinburgh firm sold Book One at nine pence, with later books for Standards Two and Three at ten pence and a shilling. Object lesson manuals and large wall sheets went with the series for classroom use.

Lessons take up the cat and the dog, buttercups, wheat, slate, chalk, the mouse, the rabbit, ivy, a tree, bricks, a donkey, and sheep. Poetical pieces, their titles in italics, sit beside the plain lessons. Children get science by looking: common animals, plants, and stones described in short, clear pieces, with pictures to fix each object in mind.
18533-the-child-at-home-the-principles-o:
John S. C. Abbott wrote this moral guide for young readers in 1833, as a follow-up to his Mother at Home. Published by the American Tract Society, it aims to stir gratitude for parents and build steady character, not merely to amuse. Abbott urges parents to read it with their children, so talk can deepen each lesson.

Chapters take up duty one theme at a time: truth telling, obedience, care for parents, and religious truth. Short tales carry each point, from George Washington and his hatchet to a child lost on the prairie and a young convict's fall. The book gives a plain window on how 1830s families taught right conduct at home.
18690-queechy-volume-i:
Elizabeth Wetherell wrote Queechy in 1852, here in the first volume of the 1854 Tauchnitz edition. It opens at Queechy, a country home ringed by pasture fields, where a girl of ten or eleven fetches her grandfather's hat and greatcoat for a wagon trip to the post office. An old mare of fourteen or fifteen years waits at the gate, in no danger of running off.

Later chapters bring Aunt Miriam, a fairy figure, an Englishman, two Bibles in Paris, a sawmill, watercress breakfasts, and society at Queechy. Wetherell writes with warmth about farm life, family, and faith. This volume starts one of her best-loved domestic novels.
18703-illustrated-catalogue-of-the-colle:
James Stevenson compiled this illustrated catalogue for the Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology, covering items gathered from Pueblo peoples of New Mexico in 1880. Town by town, from Cuyamunque, Nambe, and Pojuaque to Santa Clara, Jemez, San Juan, San Ildefonso, and Taos, it lists stone tools, clay ware, bone and horn goods, and vegetal items. Pictures show pitchers, bowls, pipes, canteens, and a blanket weaver.

Santa Clara polished black ware, white ware with colored designs, and red ware with black designs get close note. The catalogue records shapes, wares, and places with care. It remains a valuable source for Pueblo craft and museum history.
18736-illustrated-catalogue-of-the-colle:
James Stevenson compiled this illustrated catalogue for the Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology, covering items gathered in New Mexico and Arizona in 1879. Prepared for the First Annual Report but left out for want of space, it keeps the report's figure numbers, which explains gaps in the sequence. A note and a transmittal letter of January 3, 1881, open the work.

Stevenson praises ethnologist Frank H. Cushing, who stayed on with Pueblo peoples to study habits, customs, government, faith, and speech, and photographer John K. Hillers, whose plates show villages and people. General Sherman's aid gets thanks as well. The catalogue pairs with the 1880 volume as a record of early museum fieldwork.
18893-sketches-and-studies-in-italy-and-:
John Addington Symonds's sketches and studies in Italy and Greece gather three volumes of travel essays in one topographical arrangement, prepared by Horatio F. Brown at Venice in June 1898. Nothing changed except the order of the essays, so travelers could follow the ground itself.

The first volume moves from the love of the Alps and winter nights at Davos through Provence, the Cornice, and Venice. The second covers Ravenna, Umbria, Urbino, Florence, and the Medici, with Tuscan songs and Poliziano's Orfeo. The third ranges from Siena and Perugia to Amalfi, Etna, Palermo, Syracuse, and Athens. The opening essay asks why the classic nations hated mountains while modern travelers love them.
19482-the-ancient-banner-or-brief-sketch:
This Quaker volume, printed in Philadelphia in the mid eighteen hundreds, sketches persons and scenes from the early history of the Society of Friends. Its title text comes from the Psalms, on a banner given to those who fear God that truth may be displayed.

Sketches honor early Friends such as Robert Barclay of Ury, the Scotsman who turned from wealth and Paris pleasures to preach plain truth. Written in earnest, old-style verse and prose, the book served Friends as a record of their forebears' faith under trial. Other verses remember Burroughs, who drew his last breath in prison, and young Parnel, who died a martyr in a dungeon.
20289-herein-is-love-a-study-of-the-bibl:
Reuel L. Howe wrote Herein Is Love, a study of the biblical doctrine of love. Howe means the book for study groups of parents and teachers. Pastors and church students will gain new insights from it, he says. Any person keen on the Christian life is also addressed directly.

Love, in the Bible, is more than feeling, Howe argues throughout. It shapes how parents, teachers, and neighbors treat one another daily. Group use matters because such love is learned in shared life. Readers get a warm, practical study of faith's central command.
20843-an-estimate-of-the-value-and-influ:
Thomas Hill Green went to Rugby at fourteen, then to Balliol College, Oxford, in 1855. There he fell under Jowett, the famed translator of Plato. Fred Newton Scott's study opens with that life before it weighs fiction's worth.

An Estimate of the Value and Influence of Works of Fiction asks what novels do to readers. Scott, a noted teacher of English, treats fiction as a real force. He weighs its sway on morals, taste, and thought. The essay shows scholars of the 1890s taking the novel with full gravity at last.
20946-memoirs-of-the-jacobites-of-1715-a:
Many Jacobites sank into oblivion, their motives dim and their sacrifices untold, says volume one. Memoirs of the Jacobites of 1715 and 1745 vows to set that record straighter. Mrs. Catherine Thomson drew these lives to rescue names from neglect.

Two failed risings for the exiled Stuarts frame the lives told here. Lords who lost heads, lands, and homes fill the first volume's pages. Letters and family lore back the tales of loyalty and loss. Readers meet the losing side of Britain's last civil wars in human terms, not as mere rebels in a victor's book.
21196-little-masterpieces-of-american-wi:
Thomas L. Masson edited this 1903 Doubleday, Page anthology of short American humour, the first of a series of little masterpieces. Washington Irving, Oliver Wendell Holmes, and Benjamin Franklin stand at its head. Mark Twain, Josh Billings, Charles Dudley Warner, and Henry Ward Beecher also appear.

Twain even supplied a handwritten note joking that his assistant compilers chose his pieces, which is why there are not more of them. Selections come from writers like S. W. Foss, James Whitcomb Riley, and Mary Mapes Dodge. The volume collects the short comic pieces, verses, and sketches that filled American magazines and newspapers of the age.
21339-the-works-of-aphra-behn-volume-i:
Montague Summers edited this first volume of Aphra Behn's collected works in 1915, with a long memoir of her mysterious life. Behn was among the first English women to earn her living by writing. The volume holds four plays: The Rover in two parts, The Dutch Lover, and The Roundheads.

The Rover follows banished cavaliers in carnival Naples, full of disguise, duels, and courtesans with hearts. The Roundheads turns to Civil War politics under the subtitle The Good Old Cause. Summers's preface warns that early claims about Behn need hard proof before belief. His edition began the modern recovery of her work for readers and stages.
21752-my-doggie-and-i:
A man and his small, shapeless, hairy dog stand at the center of this warm Ballantyne tale. The narrator insists his pet is not a dog but a doggie, a class apart in charm. Dumps, as he is called, has short legs, long hair, and a face veiled by both. Friends laugh at him, and his master does not care at all.

Ballantyne tells how the two met on a dusty country lane and what grew between them. The book is part love letter, part comic defense of an unlovely pet. It shows the gentle side of a writer known for storms and battles. Any reader who has loved an odd dog will know exactly what he means.
22018-the-son-of-monte-cristo-volume-i:
The Son of Monte-Cristo continues Alexandre Dumas's famous tale of the Count of Monte Cristo into the next generation. This first of two volumes appeared in the thirty-volume Collier edition of Dumas's works. It opens with a marriage contract that ends in ruin. A family tragedy and a strange trial follow fast.

Benedetto the murderer escapes the prison hulks, and death sentences hang over more than one head. Old friends of the Count, Cavalcanti and Danglars among them, move through the plot. Monte-Cristo himself returns before the volume closes. Readers who finished the Count's own story get the same fare here: disguise, vengeance, and last-minute rescue.
22405-the-olden-time-series-vol-2-the-da:
The Olden Time Series, volume two, recalls the days of the spinning wheel in New England, in 1885. It gathers scraps of colonial life before factories changed home work. A motto from Hazlitt frames its backward look.

Hazlitt argues that the past, having ceased to be, counts as nothing. The future, yet to come, has never been anything either. Against that cold logic, the series preserves small old facts. Spinning wheels, home cloth, and daily customs get their due. Such antiquarian books saved details that grand histories ignored. Readers interested in early American homes will find the volume a storehouse of humble, telling particulars.
22832-the-cathedral-church-of-canterbury:
Canterbury Cathedral gets a full guidebook treatment in this second edition from the Bell's Cathedrals series. The author names his authorities up front. They include Willis on the cathedral's building history and Dean Stanley's memorials of the city and church.

Inside, readers tour the building stone by stone. The guide explains the choir, chapels, tombs, and windows, and ties each feature to the bishops, kings, and pilgrims who shaped the church. Becket's shrine and murder naturally loom large in the story. Compact and earnest, the volume was made for visitors who wanted facts in hand while they walked. It still serves that purpose well.
23100-a-budget-of-paradoxes-volume-i:
Augustus De Morgan collects cranks in A Budget of Paradoxes, volume one. De Morgan flags one large omission himself. He leaves out the famous quarrel between Sir James South and Troughton over mounting the great equatorial telescope at Campden Hill. Someday, when no living astronomer remembers the feud, the omitted sketch will make fine reading, De Morgan promises, as history and character study both.

De Morgan, a mathematician, spent years answering circle-squarers, perpetual-motion men, and other paradoxers, and this book is his museum of them. The letters are funny, sad, and endlessly inventive. Astronomy feuds like the Campden Hill quarrel show that professionals could match amateurs in stubbornness. The Budget remains the classic tour of respectable delusion, guided by a wit who pitied his specimens even while refuting them.
23424-the-flag-of-my-country-shike-yah-b:
Cecil S. King wrote this Navajo reader, with the Navajo text by Marian Nez, teacher and interpreter, and pictures by Henry Bahe, a fourth year student, all of the Carson Indian School. Issued by the Bureau of Indian Affairs as a Navajo New World Reader, it teaches the flag of the speaker's country in both tongues.

Short lines, clear pictures, and Navajo words beside English help young Navajo readers learn to read while learning civic pride. The book stands as a record of mid century bilingual schooling, made by Native teachers and students for Native children. Readers today will value it for its language, its art, and its window onto how the flag and the nation were taught in Navajo classrooms.
23469-a-history-of-the-four-georges-volu:
Justin McCarthy opened his history of the four Georges with the death of Queen Anne in seventeen fourteen, when rival claimants, statesmen, and parties plotted for the throne as the queen sank. Swift's letters show a court that acted as if Anne were immortal, while armies and emissaries moved in the shadows.

Volume one follows George the First, a German prince and Elector of Hanover more than an English king in temper, through Jacobite threats, party strife, and the settling of a new dynasty. Chapters on patriots and their victories carry the tale toward a Britain learning to live under Hanoverian rule. Readers who like history as narrative will find McCarthy's opening volume clear, lively, and full of people.
24362-the-history-of-tasmania-volume-i:
John West, minister of St. John Square Chapel, Launceston, wrote this history of Tasmania, published at Launceston in 1852, in a volume dedicated to Henry Hopkins of Hobart Town, at whose request it was undertaken. West thanks gentlemen who lent works and original papers for years, including the trustees of Lady Franklin's Museum, and credits Ronald Gunn for the section on Tasmanian zoology and F. Wales for a list of chief places.

The first volume opens with discovery: Van Diemen, governor of Batavia, and Banks obtaining Tasman's charts and journal. The discovery of Van Diemen's Land and Maria Island follow, with visits by Marion, Furneaux, Cook, Clerke, Cox, Bligh, and D'Entrecasteaux. Bass and Flinders find Bass Strait. From 1803 to 1824, occupation, Port Phillip abandoned, Buckley, Sullivan's Cove, and Collins follow. Readers get a colonial history, written close to its sources.
2437-they-and-i:
Jerome K. Jerome's They and I recounts a family's move to a country house and the small wars that follow: with servants, tradesmen, neighbors, and the house itself. The narrator, his wife, and their children muddle through repairs, gardens, and visitors, with Jerome's humor turning domestic chaos into comedy. The book is a sequel in spirit to his earlier idling essays.

The charm lies in Jerome's voice, warm and self-mocking, and in the recognizable truth of household life. Readers who enjoy gentle domestic humor will find a pleasant companion. It is Jerome at his most relaxed.
24984-little-gidding-and-its-inmates-in-:
J. E. Acland's 1903 volume, published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, tells of Little Gidding and its inmates in the time of King Charles I, under Nicholas Ferrar. The king's warm words to the household promised lasting remembrance of their work. Ferrar, born in 1592 to pious merchant parents, memorized large portions of the Bible as a boy.

At thirty-three he left the busy scenes for which he seemed suited and spent his last twelve years in seclusion at Little Gidding, directing a household devoted to good works. The book also describes the Harmonies he designed and constructed, and the embroidery his household made, patterns drawn on paper, cut out, and worked in high relief. Sold or exhibited, the work was marked as that of the 'Nuns of Little Gidding.'
25962-world-s-war-events-vol-i:
The first volume of World's War Events, compiled by Francis J. Reynolds and Allen L. Churchill, runs from the causes of the war and the invasion of Belgium in 1914 to the close of 1915. Baron Beyens opens on what caused the war, Charles Bronne tells the defense of Liège, and Sir John French covers the great retreat and the Marne. French official accounts, the race for the channel, and the last ditch in Belgium follow.

Later pieces take up why Turkey entered the war and scenes from the eastern fronts. One desert passage shows two camel riders waving white cloths at ten in the morning, then a long train of camel troops singing toward the camp, messengers of the Emir of Mecca. The volume gives the war's first years in the voices of those who fought and saw it.
26031-memoirs-and-correspondence-of-admi:
Sir John Ross, captain in the Royal Navy, writes the memoirs and correspondence of Admiral Lord de Saumarez from family papers, first volume printed by Bentley in 1838. Chapters trace the Saumarez genealogy, curious records, and branches of the family. Then comes the admiral's start: schooling, a duke's visit to Guernsey, a choice for the navy, and a place on the Solebay's books. Marriage closes the opening chapters.

Later pages turn on battle honors and a sharp exchange over second in command. Captain Ball, expecting distinction as second, heard Saumarez cry that all did their duty and there was no second in command, a remark that reached Nelson's ears. Ross tells a sailor's life from Guernsey boyhood to fleet command with documents and care.
26236-vixen-volume-i:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon's Vixen, here in volume one of the three-volume Tauchnitz edition of 1879, opens on a late October night in a pine wood. Roderick Vawdrey, gun in hand after a day's rabbit shooting, walks a broad clearing on his way home. Chapter titles promise a pretty horsebreaker, Lady Jane Vawdrey, Rorie's coming of age, and his first speech.

Later chapters bring a house of mourning, Captain Winstanley, and quarrels over right and wrong measured out in kind. The Squire's old stable yard, with its carved stone basin, roots the tale in country life. This first volume sets up a Victorian story of youth, pride, and love, with Braddon's brisk, dramatic pace.
26419-the-life-of-gordon-volume-i:
Demetrius C. Boulger's 1896 biography, the first of two volumes, traces Major-General Charles Gordon from his early service through his China campaigns. Boulger worked from Gordon's own papers and letters, lent by the general's brother Sir Henry Gordon after Gordon himself laughed that he would never read the book. The preface recalls the author telling Gordon of the plan in 1881, before Gordon was hemmed in at Khartoum.

The volume follows Gordon from the Crimea onward, with long attention to China. There peasant rebels of Kwangsi and artisans of Kwantung, joined by Triad leaders skilled in intrigue, took the title of Wang, or prince, and divided in advance the prizes of revolt. Gordon's later Equator and Soudan correspondence belongs to the story's later stages, beyond this volume's close.
26434-the-boys-of-crawford-s-basin-the-s:
Sidford F. Hamp's 1907 boys' novel tells of a mountain ranch in the early days of Colorado. The story opens at night, when the boys' father, in nightshirt and boots with lantern and rifle, wakes Joe and Phil to face Big Reuben, a grizzly bear raiding the pig-pen. Big Reuben, a notorious old criminal among ranchmen, has harmed the neighborhood for two or three years.

Later chapters follow the boys through Crawford's Basin, a hermit's warning, a wild cat's trail, an underground stream, and Tom Connor's boring for oil. An ore theft, a snow-slide, the Big Reuben vein, and the draining of the Forty Rods keep the ranch plot moving. Chase Emerson's pictures show the bear looking down on the boys from the frontispiece.
26829-the-old-helmet-volume-i:
Susan Warner's novel appeared in this authorized Tauchnitz edition at Leipzig in 1864, in two volumes, under the name of the author of Wide, Wide World. A note to the reader insists the incidents given as fact come from excellent authority, not imagination, with third parties' words left unchanged. Volume one opens among celebrated ruins, where the first thing noticed is a gleam of white teeth.

The teeth belong to Eleanor, a lively young woman with full brown hair and eyes, a frank smile, and a ready hint of mischief. She would rather be walking with a far more interesting member of her party, but Mr. Carlisle has gone home for an hour or two, leaving her on a grassy bank beside a grave gentleman she barely knows. The ruins, the shaven turf, and the old oaks frame a heroine at the start of her story.
27003-notes-and-queries-number-203-septe:
Notes and Queries number 203, for Saturday, September 17, 1853, is a fourpenny weekly where literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists swapped facts and questions. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of.

This number leads with Shakespearian correspondence, then notes on Pepys and East London topography, Picts' houses in Aberdeenshire, and folk lore from County Clare. The notes also carry heraldic notes on the arms of Granville and of Richard, King of the Romans. Queries follow on Sir Philip Warwick and the seals of Great Yarmouth, making the issue a small museum of Victorian curiosity.
27004-notes-and-queries-number-204-septe:
Saturday, September 24, 1853 brings Notes and Queries number 204, opening with extinct volcanos and mountains of gold in Scotland. J. B. Whitborne writes on Thomas Blount, author of Fragmenta Antiquitatis, and C. Forbes offers a plea for the horse under the heading Give him a Roll.

Dream testimony and Shakespeare correspondence follow, with minor notes on Bacon sentences, bottled beer, and Milton at Eyford House. Queries ask after the Earl of Leicester's portrait of 1585, the early use of tin, and St. Patrick, in the weekly's familiar blend of the learned and the curious.
27151-memoirs-and-correspondence-of-admi:
Sir John Ross's Memoirs and Correspondence of Admiral Lord de Saumarez, volume two, published in London in 1838, draws on original papers in the family's possession. The volume opens with news of the battles of July 6 and 12 reaching England, and rejoicings described in a letter from Mrs. Saumarez.

Later chapters record the promotion of Lieutenant Dumaresq, letters from Earl St. Vincent and others, and remarks on the governor and garrison at Gibraltar. Correspondence with the Spanish governor at Cadiz over red-hot balls, and the refutation of an accusation, shows Saumarez defending his conduct in print. Ross served as a captain in the Royal Navy. The book is the second of two volumes.
27373-flora-lyndsay-or-passages-in-an-ev:
Mrs. Moodie, the Susannah Moodie of Roughing It in the Bush, published this novel in two volumes with Richard Bentley in London in 1854. She dedicated it to Miss Gooding of Cromer in Norfolk. The first volume follows its heroine Flora Lyndsay through home life, new friends, and a voyage that carries her away from all she knows.

Early chapters give a matrimonial dialogue, an old captain, Flora's outfit, a ghost story heard while seeking a servant, and the last hours at home. Then come an open boat at sea, fog, a steamboat, and Edinburgh. Moodie writes Flora's eventful life with warmth and domestic detail, and the volume closes with its heroine well launched on her story.
27484-journal-of-a-visit-to-constantinop:
John Auldjo, author of The Ascent of Mont Blanc and Sketches of Vesuvius, kept this journal of a visit to Constantinople and Greek islands in the spring and summer of 1833. It was printed in London by A. Spottiswoode. A view in the Gulf of Coron fronts the volume.

Auldjo takes Gray's Letters as his motto: transcribe your little red books on the spot, since half a word fixed near the place is worth a cart load of recollection. Turkish names appear in French spelling, the lingua franca of the period, with correct Turkish spellings given at the end. The journal gives a lively, on-the-spot picture of the Ottoman capital and the islands.
27867-scientific-american-magazine-vol-2:
The September 26, 1846 issue of the Scientific American, volume two, number one, shows the young weekly journal of practical information, art, science, mechanics, chemistry, and manufactures. Published in New York by Munn and Company under editor Rufus Porter, it cost two dollars a year.

Contents include an eclipse in Arabia, the Bowie knife and its inventor, Howe's sewing machine, an electro-magnetic boat, cast-iron cannon, and the magnetic telegraph, with news of the Mexican War. The issue captures American inventive energy in the 1840s, when mechanics and manufactures filled a weekly paper.
28177-insects-and-diseases-a-popular-acc:
Rennie W. Doane, assistant professor of entomology at Stanford, wrote Insects and Disease in 1910 as a popular account of how insects spread sickness. Doane explains parasites, bacteria, and protozoa in plain words, with many photographs, and shows how a harmless kind can turn harmful. The book belongs to the American Nature Series.

Chapters trace mosquitoes and other insects to diseases they carry, and stress clean water, screens, and care of breeding places. Doane writes for general readers, not only for doctors. The book shows early public-health science at work, when insect control was becoming a chief weapon against disease.
28544-say-and-seal-volume-i:
Susan and Anna Warner, writing as Elizabeth Wetherell and Amy Lothrop, published Say and Seal in 1860, in two volumes. This Tauchnitz edition is volume one. Their preface jokes that the book ran over its mould, since two women both had to speak in it.

The public, they add, will never know which glove is right and which is left. The story opens in a shady, sunshiny town, with June breezes and a new schoolteacher's arrival, whose lodgings the school committee has arranged beforehand. Wide streets, great elms, and comfortable houses set the scene for a long, gentle tale of New England town life, faith, and courtship.
28708-practical-education-volume-i:
Maria Edgeworth and Richard Lovell Edgeworth wrote Practical Education, volume 1, in a second American edition published at Providence and Boston in 1815. The preface disowns any peculiar system to support, and therefore any temptation to attack the theories of others. Practice and experience alone, the authors say, must make education an experimental science.

They record facts about children that may seem trifling, with a minuteness that may look unnecessary, but admit no anecdote without deliberation. Rudiments of science, they argue, can be learned in conversation and from the incidents of life, with technical terms preserved by common use. Readers get a pioneering manual, modest about how much generations of labor may still require.
2907-joy-a-play-on-the-letter-i:
John Galsworthy's Joy, subtitled a play on the letter I, runs through a single midsummer day on the lawn of Colonel Hope's house near the Thames above Oxford. The Hope family, their governess Miss Beech, their daughter Letty, and guests including Maurice Lever gather under a huge old beech tree, in whose hollow darkness many things are hidden. The action stays outdoors from morning onward.

The comedy turns on a supposed mine, with the colonel declaring that no mine is any good without faith and offering a thousand pounds on sight unseen. Lever doubts, the colonel scorns the cautious Henty, and the letter I, for self, runs through the jokes. The play charms as a light Galsworthy piece, sunny on the surface and sly underneath.
29232-the-lady-s-own-cookery-book-and-ne:
A lady author, unnamed on the title page, published this cookery book in London in 1844, in its third edition, for Henry Colburn. The volume gathers a large collection of original receipts, drawn from the author's many years of observation, experience, and research, plus contributions from an extensive circle of acquaintance.

It serves cooks of grand establishments and of modest means alike. Opening sections give general directions and rules for a good dinner, followed by made dishes, meats, and vegetables. Readers get a substantial Victorian cookbook, valuable for its recipes and for its picture of how a well-run dinner table worked in 1844.
29268-the-holy-see-and-the-wandering-of-:
Thomas W. Allies wrote this history, volume six of his work on the Holy See, covering the period from Saint Leo I to Saint Gregory I. Published in London in 1888, it treats the papacy during the wandering of the nations, when peoples moved across a crumbling Roman world. Allies, author of The Formation of Christendom, builds his case from the letters of the popes.

Allies quotes Cardinal Mai's judgment that the whole administration of the church is learned in the popes' letters. From that source he traces Peter's successors standing up amid migration and change. Readers get a Victorian Catholic history of the early medieval papacy, scholarly in method and confident in its view of Rome as an anchor in unsettled times.
31901-tom-burke-of-ours-volume-i:
Charles James Lever's Tom Burke of Ours, volume one, illustrated by Phiz and Browne, depicts French military life during the Empire's brief but glorious period. Lever dedicates the book to Miss Edgeworth, noting that had the scene been laid chiefly in Ireland, he would have felt his inferiority too keenly to venture the dedication.

His preface says two impulses led him to write: the fascination Napoleon's name and exploits had exercised on his boyhood mind. The second was the favorable press notice given his scenes of soldier life in Charles O'Malley. Readers get a Napoleonic military novel, informed by Lever's personal acquaintance with men who had played great parts in the drama.
32355-with-the-children-on-sundays-throu:
Sylvanus Stall's With the Children on Sundays, through Eye-Gate and Ear-Gate into the Child-Soul, was published in Philadelphia by the Uplift Publishing Company in 1911. Earlier copyrights date to 1893, 1896, and 1907. Stall wrote What a Young Boy Ought to Know and What a Young Man Ought to Know, and C. M. Burd of New York City prepared the book's drawings and color-pictures. Its contents open with a preface and suggestions to parents.

The lessons use objects as sermons. Oyster and Crab stand for conscience, Worm in the Apple for sin in the human heart, and Wayside Weeds and Garden Flowers for neglected versus Christian children. Nuts gives God's lesson that we must work. Banks, Chart, Anchor, Husks, Iron, Pocket Rule, Magnet, Keys, Traps, Bread, Stone, Polished Stone, and Ropes continue the series, on treasures, dangers, hope, habits, and the heart. Readers get Sunday object lessons for children.
32478-tales-from-the-german-volume-i:
Nathaniel Greene's translation, published in Boston in 1837, presents tales from German authors for American readers with leisure hours to spend profitably and pleasantly. Greene, busy with official work, studied German language and literature in his spare time and translated tales taken almost at random from the thirteen volumes of Van der Velde's works. He valued them for faithful pictures of interesting history not generally familiar, told in a simple, unpretending style.

The volume opens with Arwed Gyllenstierna, a tale of the early eighteenth century by C. F. Van der Velde. In October 1718, royal counsellor Nils Count Gyllenstierna sits at his desk in his Stockholm cabinet, beginning a story of court, family, and northern Europe. Greene notes that he omitted or altered a few passages thought unsuited to American propriety.
32673-st-paul-s-epistle-to-the-romans-a-:
Charles Gore, then Bishop of Worcester, offers the first volume of his practical exposition of Romans, covering chapters one through eight. John Murray published it in 1902, after a first edition in February 1899. Gore dates Paul's letter from Corinth, in the year commonly reckoned 58, perhaps more correctly 56.

Three divisions carry the argument: sin and condemnation for all, justification by faith alone, and the accepted life that follows. Chapters weigh the second Adam, freedom from law, life in the Spirit, sonship, and the hope of creation. This is the true first volume, companion to the second volume on chapters nine to sixteen.
32674-st-paul-s-epistle-to-the-romans-a-:
Charles Gore offers a practical exposition of Paul's Epistle to the Romans, and this file holds the second volume, covering chapters nine through sixteen. Gore first defends God's dealings with the Jews, asking why Israel stands rejected yet not finally cast off.

Later divisions turn to daily conduct: self-surrender, community spirit, duty toward rulers, mutual tolerance, and unselfish care for others. Appended notes weigh faith, conscience, hell, atonement, the Fall, and baptism, making the volume both a commentary and a guide to Christian life. Gore writes for readers who want both doctrine and daily use. He links Paul's great themes to prayer, work, and neighborly care. The notes at the back help a reader follow hard terms without losing the thread.
33129-incidents-of-travel-in-yucatan-vol:
John L. Stephens's Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, volume one, published in New York in 1848 and illustrated with 120 engravings, begins the explorer's fuller account of Maya ruins. Stephens explains in his preface that his earlier Central America volume had promised a more thorough exploration of Yucatan's ruins, and that promise has now been carried out. Stephens presents the pages that follow as, in his belief, the fullest journey a stranger had ever made across that peninsula.

A frontispiece shows the Casa del Gobernador at Uxmal, and the volume carries readers through ruined cities, villages, and roads, with engravings to fix each site in the mind. Stephens's curiosity, stamina, and clear prose made his Yucatan books famous, and they brought Maya art and architecture to a wide audience. Volume one remains a classic of exploration, vivid, detailed, and full of the thrill of finding a lost world.
33151-the-expositor-s-bible-the-gospel-o:
Marcus Dods's Gospel of St. John, volume one, in the Expositor's Bible series edited by W. Robertson Nicoll and published in New York in 1891, offers a commentary on the Fourth Gospel for preachers and general readers. Dods, professor of exegetical theology at New College, Edinburgh, works through John's gospel passage by passage, explaining its teaching on word, light, life, and belief, and its difference from the other gospels. 

The commentary treats John as a theological gospel, written to lead readers to faith, and Dods keeps exposition clear without losing depth. His tone is learned but pastoral, aiming to help a reader preach or study with confidence. As a work of late Victorian biblical scholarship, volume one remains a solid guide to the first half of John's gospel, and a good companion to the second volume that completes it.
33162-joseph-in-the-snow-and-the-clockma:
Berthold Auerbach's Joseph in the Snow, and the Clockmaker, translated by Lady Wallace and published in London in 1861 as volume one of three, opens a Black Forest village story. Its contents run from an epitaph and the question is it not yet morning through a duet interrupted and resumed. They go on to a fierce family, Martina's return home, and a day of trouble. They then reach a village pastor summoned to court, the home of Schilder-David, and warm and snug in the parsonage. Later chapters bring betrothal and flight and a father searching for his son.

The volume then asks where Joseph is, following a child lost in the forest before sleep and waking in the forest mill. Auerbach writes village life with warmth, letting snow, forest, and church shape his characters.
33163-joseph-in-the-snow-and-the-clockma:
Volume two of Berthold Auerbach's Joseph in the Snow, and the Clockmaker, translated by Lady Wallace and published in London in 1861, continues the Clockmaker story. Its contents open with a good name, the mourner and his companion, and work and good deeds. They then move through each one for himself, pilgrim's adventures, and the world stepping in. They go on to the civilities of a landlord's pretty daughter, happiness dawning with a new mother speaking, and a parley with friends. Later chapters bring a dinner with Petrowitsch and the great clock playing its melodies, with fresh ones added.

Further chapters follow a good escort, lion, fox, and magpie, and young hearts with a proposal. Auerbach's Black Forest tale, told through clocks, work, and village custom, deepens here as its characters face love, loss, and new beginnings. The volume rewards readers following Joseph's story, and it shows Auerbach's art .
33164-joseph-in-the-snow-and-the-clockma:
Volume three of Berthold Auerbach's Joseph in the Snow, and the Clockmaker, translated by Lady Wallace and published in London in 1861, continues the Clockmaker story where earlier volumes left it. Its contents run from the first nail knocked in, peace in the house, and the first Sunday guest through ancient heirlooms dismissed and a new tone in the Morgenhalde. They go on to pendulums swinging together under stress on the mainspring, the axe put to the root of life, and everything gone.

Later chapters bring a beggar and money saved, another world, and a thaw that extends even to Petrowitsch before he freezes again. Annele thaws and freezes again in a stormy night, with a friend in need. Auerbach's village tale, told through clocks, houses, and seasons, reaches its later trials here. The volume rewards readers who have followed Joseph's story, and it shows Auerbach's art at full length.
33452-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-no-v:
Harper's New Monthly Magazine, number five, October 1850, volume one, gathers essays, tales, and notes for a growing American readership. Its contents include George Gilfillan on Wordsworth and on Thomas Carlyle, a gentleman beggar's story from Dickens's Household Words, and singular proceedings of the sand wasp. Other pieces treat horses, Quakers in war, and a shilling's worth of wonders.

The number captures American magazine life at mid-century, when British and American writing shared pages. Its mix suits readers who like a thick, varied monthly, from poetry to natural history. For students of periodicals, it is a rich snapshot of what educated Americans read in the autumn of 1850.
33688-tales-of-the-wonder-club-volume-i:
Dryasdust tells supernatural and marvelous tales in this first volume of Tales of the Wonder Club, illustrated by John Jellicoe and Val Prince after the author's designs. An introduction peers at the Wonder Club itself, toward the close of the last century, in a venerable Elizabethan hostelry at a Midland crossroads. It was known by the sign of Ye Headless Lady, its gables shaded by elms and beeches and its walls overgrown with ivy.

The host, Jack Hearty, robust and jovial, presides over the company that trades wonders. Illustrations promise a phantom flea, spirit lovers, a glacier king, a mermaid, a pigmy queen, a spirit leg, and a party lost in the catacombs. The tales mix ghost story, fairy lore, and clubroom yarn-spinning, in the manner of Victorian collections where friends compete to tell the strangest story of all.
33704-in-paradise-a-novel-vol-i:
Paul Heyse's novel In Paradise opens in this first volume, published in New York in 1878 as part of the Collection of Foreign Authors series. The translation notes that poems scattered through the German original were omitted, with only trifling changes otherwise. Heyse, already known to English readers through L'Arrabiata and other tales, writes here at greater length about artists, lovers, and Munich society.

Volume One sets the world that Volume Two continues. These include painters, patrons, and friends debating art, nature, and modern sentiment, with the lakeside house near Starnberg and its circle of characters waiting in the later book. Readers who enjoy German literary fiction in translation will find a novel of manners and ideas, where conversations about beauty and life carry as much weight as plot. The volume stands as a substantial introduction to Heyse's art.
33962-the-history-of-company-c-seventh-r:
Theodore Wilder wrote this history of Company C, Seventh Regiment, Ohio Volunteer Infantry, published at Oberlin in 1866. Wilder wrote at the request of surviving members, who wanted a brief story of marches, battles, and sieges, and an accurate record of each man for future years. The volume is dedicated to all whose names appear on the company roll.

Wilder aimed for a plain record rather than a grand account of patriotic deeds, noting that many others endured as much. The book preserves one Ohio company's Civil War in names and movements. It serves descendants, historians, and regimental researchers.
33973-the-mysterious-wanderer-vol-i:
Sophia Reeve wrote this novel in three volumes, with volume one printed in London in 1807 and dedicated to Lady Elizabeth Spencer. Reeve calls it a first essay, written for her own amusement during a winter season, and hopes it may plant a generous feeling or check a vicious one. The advertisement asks readers to soften their criticism.

Volume one opens the wanderer's tale in the manner of early nineteenth-century romance. Reeve writes with earnest feeling and a clear moral aim. The book gives modern readers a rare, early woman's novel in its original, unpolished form.
34083-stories-of-the-olden-time-historic:
James Johonnot compiled and arranged this school reader of olden stories, published in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago in 1889. Johonnot's preface notes that early history blends fact and fiction, with traditions distorted and enlarged by imagination and time. Myths stand first, as they stand first in time, followed by parables and fables.

Legends follow, where readers must separate the probable from the improbable and the true from the false. Greek myths, from Homer and Virgil, show how a nation's first literature grows. The book serves young readers learning to read old tales with judgment.
3701-letters-from-high-latitudes-being-s:
Lord Dufferin wrote these letters home during a voyage in 1856, when his schooner yacht Foam sailed for Iceland, Jan Mayen, and Spitzbergen. The letters mix high spirits with mishap from the first page, as illness delays the start and a shy Icelandic guide paces the coffee room like a polar bear. Dufferin, later Governor General of Canada and Viceroy of India, writes as a witty young lord seeing the far north for the first time.

Geysers, lava fields, Icelandic balls, and Arctic seas fill the later letters, along with dinners, French savants, and talk of local dress. The book charms because its author laughs at himself as often as he marvels at the sights. Readers who enjoy travel writing with jokes intact will find a fresh account of a north that then felt almost as remote as the moon.
3726-the-decameron-volume-i:
Giovanni Boccaccio wrote the Decameron in the shadow of the Black Death, and this first volume gathers its opening tales. Ten young Florentines, seven women and three men, flee the plague city for a country villa, where they pass ten days telling stories to while away the hours. Each day has a theme, and the tales range from bawdy jokes to high romance, told in turn by each member of the company.

The tales in this volume include lovers parted by violence, a lady whose beauty draws a prince, and rogues who talk their way out of ruin. Boccaccio tells each story with grace and bite, and the frame of gardens, songs, and feasts keeps the plague at a distance. Readers new to the book will find a vivid doorway into medieval Italy, witty, earthy, and humane by turns.
4055-the-future-of-the-colored-race-in-a:
An article on the future of Black Americans after slavery argues that their condition will overmaster all other questions for years to come. It recalls how the South once sought only to tolerate slavery, then made it the cornerstone of secession, a doctrine former builders had rejected.

The writer weighs what should be done with the freed slave, rejecting hasty plans such as removal by ships, and counting their cost in money and time. The piece speaks from the age of debate over freedom, citizenship, and reunion. Readers gain a direct view of how Americans of that era framed a question that shaped the nation.
4335-the-grounds-of-an-opinion-on-the-po:
The Reverend T. R. Malthus wrote this pamphlet in 1815 as an appendix to his Observations on the Corn Laws of the spring of 1814. In the earlier work he had stated, with strict impartiality, the advantages and disadvantages of restricting the import of foreign corn. Here he gives the grounds of his own opinion on that policy.

Malthus weighs both sides without hiding the case against his view, then argues for the course he thinks safest in Britain's actual circumstances. The pamphlet is a short work of applied economics, written while Parliament debated. It shows Malthus moving from analysis to advice, and it pairs naturally with his 1814 observations.
4390-a-history-of-greek-art-with-an-intr:
F. B. Tarbell wrote this history of Greek art, with an introductory chapter on art in general. The book moves from early Aegean and Geometric work through Archaic sculpture and vase painting to the classical masters and the Hellenistic age. Tarbell explains technique, style, and subject as he goes, for students and general readers.

The history suits readers who want more than pictures: it links temples, statues, and pots to the life that made them. Tarbell writes clearly, with dates and schools kept in order. The volume remains a useful survey of Greek art, from its first experiments to its wide spread across the ancient world.
4801-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
John Lothrop Motley, D.C.L., LL.D., corresponding member of the Institute of France, opens The Rise of the Dutch Republic, A History, dated 1855, with this first volume, its first part of historical introduction. An editor's note introduces the author himself: born in Dorchester, Massachusetts, in 1814, died in 1877, author of the novels Morton's Hope and Merry Mount. Motley served as United States minister to Austria from 1861 to 1867, and to England from 1869 to 1870.

The note adds that Mark Twain mentions his respect for Motley. It quotes Oliver Wendell Holmes, speaking before Boston's city authorities on July 4, 1863, on an observer placed on a national watch-tower in a foreign capital. This volume therefore begins not with the Dutch narrative itself, but with Motley's introduction and the editor's portrait of the historian behind it. Readers starting the history should begin here, before the centuries of feudal background in the second volume's introduction.
4810-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
The tenth volume of Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic covers 1566, part one, dated 1855. Chapter six opens with Francis Junius and his sermon at Culemburg House, then the Compromise, with portraits of Sainte Aldegonde, Louis of Nassau, Toison d'Or, and Charles Mansfeld. A sketch of the Compromise, the attitude of Orange, and his letter to the Duchess follow, with signers of the Compromise and indiscretion of the confederates.

Espionage over Philip by Orange, dissatisfaction of the seigniors, and Egmont's conduct join despair and emigration to England. The Request, a meeting at Breda and Hoogstraaten, and exaggerated statements in the state council follow, with the Duchess's hesitation and an assembly of notables. Debate on the Request and the inquisition, Brederode's character, and arrival of petitioners in Brussels carry the volume on. Readers get Motley's account of the Compromise and the petition of 1566.
4813-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
In 1567, the Dutch revolt against Spanish rule turns sharply against the Calvinist rebels, and John Lothrop Motley follows the crackdown town by town. Government troops crush poorly armed Calvinist forces at Lannoy and Waterlots, while officials press the siege and punish country people who sheltered them.

William of Orange stands at the center of the story. He refuses a new oath demanded by the government, offers to give up all his offices, and works to calm Antwerp during three days of tumult. Readers get a vivid account of a revolt losing its early momentum, and of the prince learning how to lead under pressure.
4815-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Spain answers the Dutch revolt with terror in 1568, and John Lothrop Motley opens this section with the machinery of that repression. The Duke of Alva's Blood Council summons Orange, Count Louis, and others, while the Inquisition proclaims death against the whole population of the Netherlands.

Imprisoned nobles Egmont and Horn face interrogation, formal charges, and pleas over jurisdiction, as their wives, fellow knights, and the emperor press for mercy. Orange replies with a published justification and quietly raises money and troops abroad. The volume captures both the cruelty of the trials and the first plans for armed resistance.
5652-thoughts-out-of-season-part-i:
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote Thoughts Out of Season, part one, in the first complete and authorized English translation edited by Oscar Levy, translated by Anthony M. Ludovici. This first volume pairs two early essays: David Strauss, the Confessor and the Writer, and Richard Wagner in Bayreuth. An editorial note and a translator's preface frame the essays.

The Strauss essay attacks a fashionable German thinker, while the Wagner essay celebrates the composer at Bayreuth as a cultural hope. Readers get Nietzsche young, polemical, and passionate, before his later aphoristic books. It suits anyone tracing how his philosophy began.
593-a-selection-from-the-writings-of-guy:
Guy de Maupassant's short stories of tragedy and comedy fill this first of three volumes, with a critical preface by Paul Bourget. Mademoiselle Fifi, The Horla, Miss Harriet, The False Gems, Simon's Papa, and A Country Excursion lead the set of twenty-seven tales. Bourget praises Maupassant's swift rise and his art of hiding himself in his work.

Maupassant writes with cold, precise prose, where a twist or a single detail unmasks pride, greed, or lust. Normandy peasants, Paris clerks, and soldiers share the stage. The volume serves as a fine entry to a master of the short tale, where life's comedy turns, in a line, to tragedy.
5997-maximilian-in-mexico-a-woman-s-remi:
Sara Yorke Stevenson recalls the French intervention in Mexico from 1862 to 1867, and the reign of Maximilian. Her volume grew from five Century Magazine articles, which Matías Romero, Mexico's minister to Washington, urged her to publish in more lasting form. She dedicates the book to his memory.

The contents run from the Triple Alliance and the Napoleonic idea through Puebla, the allies' rupture, and the French advance. They close with a cloud no bigger than a man's hand, the end of the intervention, and Maximilian's black decree of October 1865. Stevenson writes as a witness to a doomed empire.
6151-athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-i:
Edward Bulwer Lytton dedicates Athens: Its Rise and Fall, book one, to Henry Fynes Clinton. Clinton wrote the Fasti Hellenici, and Lytton thanks him for help drawn throughout his labors from that memorable work.

Lytton argues that chronology is not a dry pile of barren dates. For readers seeking true links between causes and effects, it is the explanation of events and the philosophy of facts. Clinton's Fasti throws light where chronology best repairs deficiency and elucidates obscurity in scanty authorities. This book alone is described here. Clinton's Fasti guides Lytton's dates throughout.
6606-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Charles Skinner opens his American lore set on the Hudson and its hills, where Rip Van Winkle sleeps, Catskill gnomes play, and a witch works her will. The volume lists tales from Pokepsie to Niagara, with a galloping Hessian, a storm ship, and a trapper's grim revenge among them. Each short tale ties a place name to a ghost, a trick, or a warning.

Skinner retells these stories in plain, brisk prose, as if heard from a neighbor who knows the river well. The Hudson volume sets the tone for the whole set: local, eerie, and fond of a twist. Readers who like place-based ghost lore will find this first book a lively start.
8000-the-slave-trade-domestic-and-foreig:
Henry Charles Carey wrote this economic study of the slave trade, domestic and foreign, asking why it exists and how it may be extinguished. His preface warns that his views differ widely from those generally held, both on the cause of the evil and on its cure. Carey, author of Principles of Political Economy, argues from trade, production, and national policy rather than from moral appeal alone.

The book is therefore a work of political economy applied to slavery: it treats the trade as an economic system with causes that can be changed. Readers interested in the antebellum debate will find an argument very different from the abolitionist pamphlet, and a window onto how economists of the period thought about labour, commerce, and power. Its reasoning remains provocative even where modern readers disagree.
8597-a-sportsman-s-sketches-works-of-iva:
Ivan Turgenev wrote these sketches from his hunting trips across the Russian provinces of Orel and Kaluga, in Constance Garnett's English version. A sportsman narrator walks the fields and forests, stops at villages and country houses, and records the peasants, landowners, doctors, and millers he meets. Each sketch stands alone, built around one person or one day out.

The first volume includes Hor and Kalinitch, the district doctor, the peasant owner Ovsyanikov, Biryuk the forester, and the night prairie tale of Bezhin Meadow. Beneath the hunting detail sits a sharp picture of serf life: poor huts, hard labour, and sharp differences between districts. Readers still turn to it for its close eye and its quiet case for the dignity of ordinary country people.
8645-prue-and-i:
George William Curtis tells these sketches through an old book-keeper who wears a white cravat, rarely goes to the opera, and never dines out. His only journey is from house to office, his only satisfaction doing his duty, and his only happiness in his Prue and his children. Curtis asks what romance such a life can hold, and what stories such a man can tell.

The answer unfolds in gentle, reflective pieces, where the clerk watches Aurelia smiling in the opera boxes, holding her court of love, youth. Beauty, and finds his own quiet life no poorer by comparison. Prue and I is a mid-Victorian meditation on contentment, marriage, and the dignity of ordinary work. It suits readers who like reflective essays, and it preserves a New York of clerks, families, and small pleasures now long gone.
8667-cetywayo-and-his-white-neighbours-r:
H. Rider Haggard, before his novels made him famous, wrote this 1882 political argument about Zululand, Natal, and the Transvaal. The book defends Cetshwayo, the Zulu king. Attacks British dealings with the Boers, quoting a speaker who insists no British government, Whig or Tory, would dare hand the Transvaal back. Haggard writes as a man who knew South Africa on the ground, not from London clubs.

Chapters lay out recent events, treaties, and border disputes, arguing that British policy had wronged both Zulus and loyal settlers. The prose is blunt, partisan, and urgent, aimed at changing minds at home. Historians read it as a key early statement of Haggard's South African views. General readers get a vivid, if one-sided, account of how empire looked to a young Englishman living among its consequences.
8821-to-the-gold-coast-for-gold-a-person:
Richard F. Burton and Verney Lovett Cameron tell their gold-seeking journey to West Africa in this first volume. Dedicated to James Irvine of Liverpool, praised for courage and energy in opening and working the golden lands of western Africa. A Shakespeare line, much have I travelled in the realms of gold, heads the dedication. Burton's preface recalls his earlier Wanderings in West Africa, written in 1862 and published anonymously in 1863.

Gold workings in Dinkira, Tueful, Wasa, and especially Akim, the hill region north of Accra, drew the travellers, where local people still worked the mines. The narrative mixes exploration, mining detail, and Victorian judgments about African societies. Burton's fame as explorer and translator gives the book its pull, while modern readers must weigh its colonial attitudes. It remains a vivid, firsthand record of a gold rush that never quite became one.
9441-helbeck-of-bannisdale-volume-i:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote Helbeck of Bannisdale, a novel of faith and love in two volumes, of which this is the first. Alan Helbeck, a devout Catholic squire, meets a young Protestant woman in the marsh lands of the north. The tale weighs what faith costs when it bars a marriage. Ward, a best-selling Victorian novelist, sets the clash in a stern, wet landscape.

Volume one opens on the Flent valley roads and peat mosses, where Helbeck walks and broods. His creed, his pride, and his love pull hard in three ways at once. The novel asks whether a true believer can bend for love, and what bending would cost his soul. A reader gets a grave, thoughtful romance of conscience, class, and creed in late Victorian England.
9633-sir-george-tressady-volume-i:
Volume one of Mrs. Humphry Ward's Sir George Tressady opens after an election triumph at Market Malford.
