George, joyous and excited, peers through his carriage's back window at a cheering crowd, torches, and closed shops under a wintry sky. The new town hall's lantern belfry rises in the distance. Ward dedicates the book to her brother William Thomas Arnold.

Part one follows George from hustings to Parliament, society, and a marriage shaped by politics and pride. Ward writes with care for motive, class, and public life. A reader gets the first half of a major Victorian political novel, rich in election color and domestic drama.
9756-leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-:
Book one of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Leila, or The Siege of Granada, opens in the summer of 1491. Ferdinand and Isabel's armies invest Granada, while moonlight touches the Sierra Nevada and the Spanish camp. Inside the Moorish city, groups linger to lutes and tales, half heedless of the siege. The enchanter and the warrior, named in chapter one, frame the tale.

Leila's story blends romance, faith, and war at the fall of Moorish Spain. Lytton writes with rich, romantic color, favoring moonlit scenes and high feeling. A reader gets the first book of a historical romance, where a city's last summer glows before its fall.
9782-female-scripture-biography-volume-i:
Francis Augustus Cox wrote Female Scripture Biography in 1831, with an essay on what Christianity has done for women. Cox quotes The Ladies' Calling: women deserve higher thoughts of themselves, not the world's injurious estimates. His preface hopes that devotional books, however many, may suit diverse tastes. Volume one, printed in Boston, opens his lives of Bible women.

The lives that follow present scriptural heroines as models of faith, courage, and worth. Cox writes for readers seeking devotion and example. A reader gets an early Victorian work of women's religious biography, earnest and respectful, and a window on how Bible women were honored then.
9971-the-dramatic-works-of-gerhart-haupt:
This first volume of Gerhart Hauptmann's dramatic works, edited by Ludwig Lewisohn in 1912, gathers his early social dramas in authorized translation. Hauptmann, who would win the Nobel Prize, brought working people and their speech onto the German stage.

The volume holds Before Dawn, a play of new ideas clashing with old ways, and The Weavers, translated by Mary Morison, his famous drama of Silesian weavers driven to revolt. Together they launched naturalism in German theatre. Readers get the two plays that made Hauptmann's name, in clear English versions for the stage.
a-history-of-greek-art-with-an-introduct:
F. B. Tarbell wrote A History of Greek Art as a compact survey for students and general readers. Tarbell begins outside Greece, with an introductory chapter on art in Egypt and Mesopotamia. A second chapter treats prehistoric art on Greek soil. Only then does the main account of classical art begin.

Architecture receives one broad chapter before sculpture takes over the book. Tarbell follows sculpture through its archaic period, a transitional phase, and the great age of the fifth and fourth centuries. The Hellenistic period, when Greek art spread widely, closes the sculpture story. A final chapter covers Greek painting, the art least preserved today. Clear period divisions and dated ranges make the volume a handy map of temples, statues, and styles.
a-selection-from-the-writings-of-guy-de-:
Guy de Maupassant's short stories fill this book. It is the first volume of a three-volume selection. A critical preface by Paul Bourget comes first. An introduction by Robert Arnot follows. Both are credited on the title page. The contents list twenty-seven stories. They include Mademoiselle Fifi, The Horla, and Miss Harriet. The False Gems, Simon's Papa, and The Diary of a Madman are also here.

Bourget praises how fully Maupassant hides himself in his work. He recounts the fast rise that began under Zola's circle in 1880. Fame came fast. Illness struck the writer down at his peak. The stories move between Normandy peasants and Paris clerks. They touch soldiers of the Franco-Prussian War. The late tales add haunted men who tell their own dread. Irony and tight form mark them all.
a-sportsman-s-sketches-works-of-ivan-tur: Ivan Turgenev opens his sportsman's sketches in this first volume, translated from the Russian by Constance Garnett. The contents include Hor and Kalinitch, Yermolai and the miller's wife, Raspberry Spring, the district doctor, and the peasant proprietor Ovsyanikov. The first sketch contrasts Orel peasants, bent and sullen in aspen hovels, with Kaluga peasants in roomy pine cottages, setting the pattern of close observation that runs through the book.
a-treatise-of-daunses-wherin-it-is-shewe: An anonymous writer of 1581 argues in this treatise that dances are, as it were, accessories and dependants annexed to whoredom. Plays, the author adds by the way, are joined and knit together in a rank or row with dances, and the abuse of plays ought not to be among Christians. It takes Saint Paul's charge to possess one's vessel in holiness and honour. The tract answers those who call dancing a thing indifferent with a case for its great hurt to the commonwealth.
abraham-lincoln-volume-i: John Torrey Morse Junior writes the first volume of his life of Abraham Lincoln in the American Statesmen series, published in 1899. The contents run from the raw material and the start in life through love, a duel, law, and Congress, north and south, and the Lincoln-Douglas joint debate. Election, interregnum, the beginning of war, and a real president without a real battle lead on. The first act of the McClellan drama carries Lincoln to foreign affairs and war's opening.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-i:
Barbier de Meynard began the complete French version of the Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi in 1861. His Les Prairies d'Or, the Meadows of Gold, ran to nine tomes by 1877, made with Pavet de Courteille for the Société Asiatique. This first tome opens the set. Al-Masudi, the tenth-century traveler of Baghdad, is the author.

In his opening books the author ranges over the creation, the shape of the earth, the seas, and the old kings of Persia and the east. He writes as a man who has sailed the Indian Ocean and asked questions in every port. The French text carries notes for names and places. This is the full Masudi that Sprenger's English start never finished.
alcibiades-i:
Plato's dialogue, translated by Benjamin Jowett, shows Socrates meeting the young Alcibiades just as the brilliant youth prepares to enter Athenian politics. The prefatory appendix warns that the dialogue may be spurious, a doubt scholars still discuss. Socrates asks a simple question: what will Alcibiades advise the city about, and what does he actually know?

The talk turns to justice, advantage, and the need to know oneself before ruling others. Alcibiades, spoiled by praise, finds his confidence quietly taken apart. The dialogue reads as a warning portrait of talent without wisdom, made sharper by what Athens later suffered from Alcibiades himself. Jowett's notes place the work among Plato's disputed writings.
analyzing-character-the-new-science-of-j: Katherine Melvina Huntsinger Blackford, with Arthur Newcomb, presents analyzing character as the new science of judging men, treating misfits in business, the home, and social life. The book claims that face, head, and bearing reveal fitness for work and marriage. As a period work of applied psychology, it reflects early twentieth-century faith in character reading.
athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-i:
Athens: Its Rise and Fall, Book I, by Edward Bulwer Lytton, opens his five book history of the Athenian people. Lytton dedicates the work to Henry Fynes Clinton, author of the Fasti Hellenici, the great chronological study of Greece. In the dedication he argues a point about chronology. It is no dry list of dates. It is the explanation of events, the philosophy of facts. He thanks Clinton for guidance through the scanty authorities left behind.

Book I covers the ground before the laws. It treats the land and early peoples of Attica. Kings and heroes follow. So does the gathering of villages into one city. The first frames of law and religion close it. Lytton writes as a novelist turned historian, giving institutions a human infancy.
britannica-1911-abbas-i:
Abbas the First of Egypt receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbas, son of Tusun and grandson of Mehemet Ali, fought in Syria under Ibrahim Pasha as a young man. Ibrahim's death in 1848 made him regent, and his grandfather's death in 1849 gave him the pashalik.

Reaction ruled his reign: trade monopolies fell, factories and schools closed, and the army shrank to nine thousand men. Nubar Pasha still called him a true Turkish gentleman of the old school. Shut in his palace, he barred plundering adventurers, yet let Britain build the Alexandria-to-Cairo railway. Two slaves murdered him at Benha Palace in July 1854. His uncle Said followed him.
britannica-1911-abd-ul-hamid-i:
Abd-ul-Hamid the First receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abd-ul-Hamid, sultan of Turkey, was born in 1725 and succeeded his brother Mustafa the Third in 1773. Long palace confinement had left him pious and peace-loving, a stranger to state affairs at his accession.

War came at once: defeat at Kozluja forced the treaty of Kuchuk Kainarji in 1774, the most disastrous Turkey ever signed, the entry holds. Crimea's loss followed as Russia moved to absorb it whole. Small gains in Syria and the Morea could not balance the account. War with Russia and Austria reopened in 1787; Ochakov fell in 1788. Four months later, in April 1789, the sultan died at sixty-four, his reign a ledger of loss.
britannica-1911-agrippa-herod-i:
Agrippa, Herod I, king of Judea from about 10 B.C. to A.D. 44, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of Aristobulus and Berenice, he was a grandson of Herod the Great. His full name was Marcus Julius Agrippa. Sent to Rome after his father's murder, he grew close to Tiberius and to the emperor's son Drusus.

When Drusus died, Agrippa's reckless spending left him deep in debt and forced him out of Rome. His uncle Herod the Tetrarch made him overseer of markets at Tiberias, then support stopped. Back in Rome he befriended Gaius, the future Caligula, and favour restored him. He gained a kingdom matching Herod the Great's in size, returned to Judea, and governed to the Jews' great satisfaction, noted for zeal toward Judaism.
britannica-1911-ahmed-i:
Ahmed I, sultan of Turkey from 1589 to 1617, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of Mahommed III, he succeeded in 1603 as the first Ottoman sultan to reach the throne before his majority. He showed a kindly, humane temper by refusing to kill his brother Mustafa. Mustafa, spared in this way, eventually succeeded him.

Early in the reign Ahmed showed decision and vigour, but his later conduct gave the lie to that promise. Wars in Hungary and Persia ended badly for Turkey. The peace of Sitvatorok in 1606 gave Ottoman prestige its first check, since Austria's yearly tribute was abolished. Ahmed then gave himself to pleasure, corruption spread through the public service, and discipline in the army decayed. Tobacco, the entry notes, entered Turkey during his reign.
britannica-1911-bahadur-shah-i:
Bahadur Shah I was a Mogul emperor of Hindustan from 1707 to 1712, son and successor of Aurangzeb. At his father's death the eldest surviving son, Prince Muazim, was governing Kabul, while his next brother, Azam Shah, took up the functions of royalty in his absence.

Muazim marched down from Kabul and, with notable generosity, offered to share the empire with Azam. The offer refused, the brothers met on the plains of Agra, where Azam was beaten and killed. Muazim then took the throne as Bahadur Shah. He was sixty-four and died five years later. Even in that short reign the empire was falling apart, the entry says, under Sikh and Mahratta inroads and inner quarrels.
britannica-1911-basil-i:
Basil I, called the Macedonian (died 886), was a Byzantine emperor profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born to an Armenian family settled in Macedonia, he spent part of his boyhood as a captive in Bulgaria. He escaped, and rose as a groom in the household of a relative of the Caesar Bardas. Danielis, a wealthy lady of Patrae, endowed him with a fortune. A wrestling victory then won him the notice of the emperor Michael III.

Ruthlessness carried Basil to the throne. He became Michael's boon companion and chamberlain, murdered Bardas with the emperor's consent in 866, and was raised to imperial rank weeks later. In 867 he had Michael himself assassinated and reigned alone. The adventurer then showed a born ruler's gifts for administration. He founded the Macedonian dynasty and began the legal revival, completed by his successor, that renewed Justinian's law. Under him the empire became Europe's strongest power.
britannica-1911-bayezid-i:
Bayezid I (1347–1403), an Ottoman sultan, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was surnamed Yilderim, “Lightning,” for the great speed of his movements in war. He followed his father Murad I, murdered on the field of Kossovo in 1389. He marked his rise by ordering the killing of his brother Yakub. His arms won both in Europe and in Asia, and he was the first Ottoman ruler to be styled “sultan,” a title the Abbasid caliph granted him.

One defeat undid the whole reign. After crushing the knights of Christendom at Nikopoli in 1396, he pressed into Greece. Constantinople would likely have fallen had the emperor not bought him off. Then Timur, the Mongol conqueror, met him at Angora. Bayezid was utterly beaten, taken prisoner, and died in captivity some months later, in March 1403.
britannica-1911-carlos-i:
Carlos I (1863–1908) was king of Portugal. He was the third Braganza-Coburg sovereign of that country. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his reign. He was born on 28 September 1863. His father was King Louis I of Portugal. His mother was Maria Pia, daughter of Victor Emmanuel of Italy. At about twenty he travelled widely, visiting England in 1883.

On 22 May 1886 Carlos married Marie Amélie of Orléans. Her father was the comte de Paris. On his father's death, in October 1889, he took the throne. That year Britain protested Portuguese moves in South Africa. Relations between the two countries were greatly strained. The king's attitude was one of conciliation throughout. His firm, temperate speech to the Cortes helped the peace party. He was a patron of science and literature himself. He was also an artist of some repute, the entry says.
britannica-1911-emanuel-i:
Emanuel I, in Portuguese Manoel (1469–1521), was the fourteenth king of Portugal, surnamed the Happy. He was the son of Duke Ferdinand of Vizeu and Beatrice of Beja, and was born at Alcochete in 1469. In 1495 he became king in succession to his cousin John II. He married three times, each time into the ruling house of Castile.

Emanuel's reign is noted for the spread of the Portuguese voyages and their chain of trading posts. Vasco da Gama opened the all-sea route to India, Cabral landed in Brazil, and Corte-Real sailed to Labrador in his years. Trade links opened with Persia and China, bringing Portugal wealth and colonial primacy. The entry also marks his fierce religious zeal. He persecuted the Jews he had first been ready to tolerate, pressed for a joint crusade against the Turks, and built twenty-six monasteries and two cathedrals. He died at Lisbon on 13 December 1521.
britannica-1911-ernest-i:
Ernest I, duke of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha (1784–1844), was the son of Francis, duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, born on 2 January 1784. When his father died in December 1806, Coburg was held by Napoleon as conquered land. Ernest gained his inheritance only after the peace of Tilsit in July 1807. 

After Leipzig, Ernest commanded the fifth army corps and reduced Mainz by blockade, and in 1815 he led the Saxon troops. The congress of Vienna rewarded him with the principality of Lichtenberg, which he sold to Prussia in 1834. In 1826 he received the duchy of Gotha in a family division and took the style Ernest I of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. The entry praises his work for his lands' trade, schools, and constitution. His reign is chiefly marked by the rise of the house of Coburg, through his brother Leopold's Belgian throne and his sister Victoria's daughter, Queen Victoria.
britannica-1911-flavian-i:
Flavian I, who died in 404, was bishop or patriarch of Antioch, born about 320, most probably in that city. He inherited great wealth but chose to give his riches and talents to the service of the church. With Diodorus, later bishop of Tarsus, he backed the Catholic faith against the Arian bishop Leontius. The two friends gathered their followers outside the city walls for worship. In those meetings, says Theodoret, antiphonal singing was first used in church services.

When Meletius became bishop of Antioch in 361 he raised Flavian to the priesthood. On Meletius's death in 381 Flavian was chosen to succeed him. Schism still split the church, though, and Rome and Egypt refused to know him while a rival line held part of the flock. After the rival Evagrius died about 393, Flavian kept that line from gaining a successor, slowly healing the breach before his own death.
britannica-1911-francis-joseph-i:
Francis Joseph I (born 1830), emperor of Austria, king of Bohemia and apostolic king of Hungary, was the eldest son of the archduke Francis Charles. He was born on 18 August 1830. His mother, the archduchess Sophia, daughter of Maximilian I of Bavaria, was a woman of great ability and strong character. In the years after the emperor Francis died she was probably the most influential person at court. The emperor Ferdinand, who succeeded in 1835, was unfit for his duties and childless. Francis Joseph stood next in line.

During the disturbances of 1848 the young archduke spent time in Italy. Under Radetzky, at Santa Lucia, he had his first experience of warfare. At the end of that year he came to the throne. The long entry, written while he still reigned, follows his long reign.
britannica-1911-frederick-augustus-i:
Frederick Augustus I (1750-1827), king of Saxony, was born at Dresden on 23 December 1750 and followed his father in 1763 under a guardian. Declared of age in 1768, he married Maria Amelia of Zweibrücken the next year. Careful, methodical, and fair, he earned the surname the Just, and cut taxes, imposts, and the army.

He sided with Frederick the Great in the Bavarian succession war of 1778 and gained six million florins at the peace of Teschen. He declined the Polish crown in 1791 and joined Prussia against France in 1806. After Jena he made peace at Posen, took the royal title, and entered the Confederation of the Rhine, while Napoleon made him grand-duke of Warsaw in name more than fact. Captured after Leipzig in 1813, he lost three-fifths of his lands to Prussia yet was welcomed home, and spent his last years rebuilding his kingdom.
britannica-1911-hatto-i:
Hatto I (c. 850–913) was archbishop of Mainz. He came from a Swabian family. Reichenau monastery probably educated him. He became its abbot in 888. King Arnulf appointed him archbishop in 891. People called him the heart of the king. He presided over the synod of Tribur in 895. He accompanied Arnulf to Italy twice. Pope Formosus received him with great favour.

Arnulf's death in 899 made Hatto regent of Germany. He guarded the young Louis the Child. He also gathered abbeys for himself, Ellwangen and Lorsch. Accusations of betraying Adalbert of Babenberg dogged him. In 911 he helped elect Conrad of Franconia king. Saxons blamed him for Conrad's hostility to Duke Henry. A murder plot against Henry was laid at his door. He died on 15 May 913. Saxony long remembered him with abhorrence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adalbert-i:
Adalbert I, or Albert, was Archbishop of Mainz from 1111 to 1137, from the family of the Counts of Saarbrucken. He served as imperial chancellor under Germany's Henry IV and Henry V. In 1110 he headed an embassy to Rome for Henry V's coronation. He helped bring about the Treaty of Sutri, exploiting the character of Pope Paschal II, a saintly man but no diplomat. Henry then imprisoned the pope harshly for two months over a disagreement.

Fearing schism, Paschal granted Henry the privilege of conferring ring and staff on bishops elected with papal consent, then crowned him in St. Peter's in 1111. Henry named Adalbert archbishop in reward for his part in the intrigue. From the day he received the insignia, Adalbert changed. The ex-chancellor, lately blindly zealous for the emperor, became a brave and loyal defender of church and pope. He died in 1137 after long faithful service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eanbald-i:
Eanbald the First, earliest York archbishop of that name, must not be confused with Eanbald the Second. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry leaves his birth date unknown and sets his death on 10 August 796. Most of his life likely passed in the monastery of York, where with Alcuin he oversaw the rebuilding of the minster. Albert, in his declining years, chose Eanbald as coadjutor and successor.

He took the archbishopric in 782 and first sought the pallium, which Alcuin fetched from Rome. Troubled times did not stop him from sustaining York's school and treasuring its great library. In 791 he consecrated Baldulf as bishop of Whithorn, and his last public act, crowning Eardulf king of Northumbria in June 796, closed a faithful reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugenius-i:
Eugenius I was Archbishop of Toledo in Visigothic Spain, holding the see from 636 until his death in 647. Like his predecessor Justus, he had studied under Helladius at the monastery of Agli. The entry remembers him as a virtuous and intelligent bishop. It also notes his fame as an astronomer and his skill with numbers, a rare note in a short life of a seventh-century prelate.

His public work lay in the councils of Toledo. In that age these councils served as national diets called by the king. Lay lords sat beside bishops, and temporal affairs were settled as well as spiritual ones. Eugenius presided at the fifth council, called in 636 by King Chintila to confirm his rise to the throne. He also took part in the sixth and seventh councils, the last of which ordered Toledo's bishops to spend one month each year in the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eutychius-i:
Eutychius I was Patriarch of Constantinople in the sixth century, born about 512 in Phrygia and dead on Easter Day 582. A monk and then archimandrite at Amasea, he impressed Justinian I when sent to the capital on business in 552. On the death of Patriarch Mennas that same year, the emperor had him elected successor at once. The great quarrel of the Three Chapters, over anathemas against three long-dead theologians suspected of Nestorianism, was then raging.

Eutychius presided at the Fifth General Council at Constantinople in 553, which confirmed Justinian's edicts despite Pope Vigilius, and he composed its decree. In 562 he dedicated the new church of Sancta Sophia. He later resisted Justinian's decree favoring the Aphthartodocetes, who held Christ's body incorruptible, and was deposed and banished in 565. Recalled in 577, he died after renouncing a late error denying the resurrection of the body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-i:
Francis I, born at Cognac on 12 September 1494 and dead at Rambouillet on 31 March 1547. He was King of France from 1515 and a central figure of the Renaissance wars. Son of Charles of Orleans, Count of Angouleme, and Louise of Savoy, he succeeded his cousin Louis XII, who left no male heir, since Salic law barred succession through women. His victory at Marignano in 1515 over the Swiss defending Milan made his name in Italy.

At Bologna he settled with Leo X the concordat that governed the French Church until the Revolution. It began a long drive to make royal power preponderant over nobles, bishops, and lords. After Maximilian's death in 1519 he contested the imperial crown with Charles of Austria, who became Charles V. France found itself ringed by Habsburg lands on three sides, a rivalry that shaped the rest of his reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-i:
Frederick I, German king from 1152 and later emperor, took Charlemagne as his model and set out to restore imperial power to its full reach. Son of Frederick of Swabia and Judith, daughter of Henry the Black, he was born around 1123 and crowned at Aachen in March 1152. The Catholic Encyclopedia entry paints a ruler of striking presence, quick judgment, and firm purpose.

His program began at home: touring his realm, making peace between rival princes, and winning back a royal voice in choosing bishops. His chief counselor for eleven years was Rainald von Dassel, archbishop of Cologne and imperial chancellor, a statesman in whom the bishop nearly vanished. Frederick's long reign, ending with his death in June 1190, shaped both Germany and its uneasy ties with the papacy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-i:
Hermann I, landgrave of Thuringia from 1190 to 1217, is best remembered as a patron of medieval German poets. Second son of Ludwig the Iron, he took up residence first at Neuenburg and then at the Wartburg near Eisenach. His court gave poets a home and a hearing, and his name stays tied to the flowering of German court poetry in his time.

His politics were far less steady than his patronage. He fought Henry the Lion and joined a crusade in 1197. He also shifted sides more than once in the wars between Philip of Swabia and Otto of Brunswick, so his lands were often overrun and laid waste. In 1211 he joined the princes who chose Frederick of Hohenstaufen at Nuremberg after Otto was excommunicated. The entry weighs both sides of a ruler famed for culture and faulted for shifting loyalties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isabella-i:
Isabella the Catholic was queen of Castile. She was born at Madrigal de las Altas Torres on 22 April 1451. She died just before noon on 26 November 1504 at La Mota castle in Medina del Campo. She was daughter of John II by his second wife, Isabella of Portugal. She lost her father at little more than three. Her mother raised her piously at Arévalo until thirteen. Her brother Henry IV then took her and her brother Alfonso to court.

The move, ostensibly to finish her education, aimed in truth to keep the royal children from becoming rallying points for discontented nobles. Castilian nobles had grown powerful through repeated long minorities and weak kings, and Isabella's youth unfolded inside that struggle for the crown. The entry follows her from guarded childhood toward the throne she would share and reshape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-justinian-i:
Justinian I, emperor from 527 to 565, set out to restore the Roman Empire to greatness, power, and unity. Born about 483 at Tauresium in Illyricum, he was Justin I's nephew, son of the emperor's sister Vigilantia. During his uncle's reign he became the state's chief power, was proclaimed consul in 521, and became Augustus in April 527. His thirty-eight-year reign divides into military triumphs, legal work, church policy, and building.

His general Belisarius routed the Persians at Daras in 530, destroyed the Vandal kingdom in Africa in 533, and retook Sicily, Rome, and Ravenna from the Goths. By 540 all Italy up to the Frankish frontier stood reunited to the empire, though a Gothic revolt under Totila required a second conquest, finished by 553. Narses then became the first Exarch of Italy. The Persian war, by contrast, ended in a peace on fairly equal terms in September 531.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximilian-i:
Maximilian I, Duke of Bavaria from 1598 and Elector from 1623 to his death at Ingolstadt in 1651, was born at Munich in 1573. Son of the zealous Catholic William V and Renate of Lorraine, he was strictly schooled at home and studied law, history, and maths at Ingolstadt from 1587 to 1591. Visits to Prague, Naples, Rome, Loretto, and Einsiedeln rounded his training. He took the government in 1597 at his father's wish.

His land was deep in debt from lax predecessors, so he cut spending, raised revenues, worked the salt mines himself, and taxed without heeding the powerless estates. The treasury recovered and built a reserve that survived even hard times. He kept internal order with laws of 1616 and gave great care to the army. The entry, which justly grants him the name Great, follows his services to Bavaria and the Catholic Church through the Thirty Years' War era.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-methodius-i:
Methodius I, Patriarch of Constantinople from 842 to 846, defended images in the second Iconoclast persecution. He was born at Syracuse toward the eighth century's end and died at Constantinople on 14 June 846. Son of a rich family, he came young to Constantinople seeking a court place, but a monk turned his mind, and he entered a monastery. 

The monks nearly all stood firm for images, and Methodius stood out in defiance of the government. In 815 Patriarch Nicephorus I was deposed and banished for resisting the Iconoclast laws, and Theodotus I was intruded in his place. That year Methodius went to Rome, apparently sent by the deposed patriarch, to report to Pope Paschal I. He stayed until Leo V was murdered in 820 and Michael II succeeded. Bearing a papal letter urging Michael to restore Nicephorus, Methodius returned, was scourged with seventy stripes, and exiled to Antigoni island.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-adrian-i:
Pope Adrian I reigned from about 1 February 772 to 25 December 795, a pontificate of twenty-three years, ten months, and twenty-four days. No successor of Saint Peter matched its length for a thousand years, until Pius VI surpassed it by six months. Adrian was a Roman of noble birth and majestic stature, esteemed for piety and learning under Paul I and Stephen III.

His temporal policy was steadfast resistance to Lombard aggression. He freed or recalled the victims of the chamberlain Paul Afiarta, who served the Lombard king Desiderius, and ordered Afiarta's arrest after the murder of a papal official. When Desiderius threatened all Italy and sought the anointing of Carloman's sons against Charles, later Charlemagne, Adrian chose resistance and looked to the Franks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict:
Pope Benedict I, the first pontiff of that name, is a figure about whom practically nothing is known. His birth date is unknown, and he died on 30 July 579. He was a Roman, son of Boniface, and the Greeks called him Bonosus. Lombard ravages made it hard to reach the emperor at Constantinople, who claimed the right to confirm papal elections.

Nearly eleven months passed between John III's death and the imperial confirmation of Benedict's election on 2 June 575. He reigned four years, one month, and twenty-eight days. Almost his only recorded act is the grant of an estate, the Massa Veneris near Minturnae, to Abbot Stephen of Saint Mark's near Spoleto. Famine followed the Lombards, and he died amid efforts to cope with it, buried in the sacristy vestibule of old Saint Peter's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-callistu:
Pope Saint Callistus I, martyr, died about 223 after an episcopate of five years. His contemporary Julius Africanus dates his accession to 218 or 219, the first or second year of Elagabalus, and Eusebius agrees on five years. His Acts are spurious, but he appears in the fourth-century Depositio Martirum, good evidence he truly was a martyr, though he lived in peace under Alexander Severus, whose mother was a Christian.

Our chief knowledge comes from bitter enemies, Tertullian and the antipope Hippolytus, author of the Philosophumena. They say Callistus, slave of Carpophorus, lost money entrusted to his bank, fled, was caught, and was set to the hand-mill. Freed at the brethren's plea, he courted death by insulting Jews at their synagogue. Legend places his church, Saint Callistus, by Santa Maria in Trastevere, with a well where his body was thrown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-honorius:
Pope Honorius I, a Campanian consecrated 27 October 625 in succession to Boniface V, reigned from 625 to 12 October 638. He is notorious as a heretic condemned by the Sixth General Council in 680. The Monothelite question reached him about 634 in a letter from Sergius, Patriarch of Constantinople. Sergius told how Heraclius in Armenia in 622 had used the phrase one operation of the Incarnate Word against a Monophysite.

Cyrus of the Lazi doubted the phrase, and Sergius advised caution. Made Patriarch of Alexandria in 630, Cyrus used it to reunite many Monophysites to the Church. Former foes of Leo and Chalcedon praised both aloud. Sophronius objected, and Sergius, hoping to save the Alexandrine union, asked both sides to drop talk of one or two operations. He laid the whole matter before the pope. The entry follows his reply, the Ecthesis of Heraclius, the Type of Constans, and the sense in which the council condemned him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent:
Pope Innocent I, of unknown birth date, died on 12 March 417 after an energetic reign zealous for the whole Church's welfare. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a native of Albano, son of Innocentius, raised among the Roman clergy in the Roman Church's service. After Anastasius died in December 401 he was unanimously chosen Bishop of Rome by clergy and people.

Little survives of his Roman administration, but his zeal for purity of faith and discipline is well attested. He took several churches from the Novatians and banished the Photinian Marcus from the city. Through the matron Vestina's generosity he built and endowed the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, the old Titulus Vestinae now called San Vitale. Alaric's siege and sack of Rome in 410 fell in his reign. He joined the embassy to Honorius at Ravenna seeking peace, failing, so that he could not return before the city fell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-marinus-:
Marinus I was the son of the priest Palumbo. He was born at Gallese. He joined the Roman church at twelve. He was sent three times as envoy to Constantinople. On one mission he was jailed for standing firm on his orders. He served as bishop of Cære, treasurer, and archdeacon. He was elected on the day John VIII died in December 882.

Though a bishop, he was an unusual choice for pope. He reversed his predecessor's censure of Bishop Formosus. He held firm against Photius of Constantinople. The entry untangles his confusion with Martin I. That mix-up later made historians misnumber him. It also notes his gifts to Reims and to King Alfred's English school at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paschal-:
Paschal I was the son of the Roman Bonosus. He trained at the Lateran Palace. He looked after pilgrims as head of St Stephen's monastery. He was unanimously elected in January 817. That was the day after Stephen IV died. He at once won a document from Emperor Louis. The Pactum Ludovicianum confirmed the rights and lands of the Holy See.

He stayed friendly with the Frankish court. He sent rich gifts to Lothair's wedding. He crowned Lothair emperor at Rome in April 823. Yet he opposed Frankish sovereignty over Rome itself. The entry then turns to the palace feud with officials who backed the Franks. It ends with Paschal's death in the spring of 824.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paul-i:
Paul I was the brother of Stephen II. Both were pupils at the Lateran Palace. Paul was elected by a large majority at once after Stephen's burial in April 757. He was consecrated on 29 May. He had already handled delicate business for his brother. That included reclaiming Roman cities seized by Lombard kings Aistulf and Desiderius.

He kept Stephen's line toward the Frankish king Pepin. He held papal rule over Rome and central Italy. He held it against Lombards and the Eastern Empire. He traded warm gifts with Pepin. He thanked the king for a baptismal cloth sent at his daughter's birth in 758. The entry follows his diplomacy to his death at Rome in June 767.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pelagius:
Pelagius I came from a noble Roman line. His father John seems to have governed a civil district of Italy as vicar. He first appears at Constantinople with Agapitus I. Just before dying there, Agapitus made him nuncio of the Roman church in 536. Empress Theodora schemed for the Monophysite heresy. Her intrigues led Belisarius to depose Silverius. Pelagius was pressed to rush east and block Silverius's recall. He failed.

He gained great influence with Emperor Justinian. He chose the orthodox Paul for Alexandria in 540 and deposed him two years later. He helped condemn Origen and returned to Rome in 543. At St Peter's he swore on the Gospels that he had done Vigilius no harm. His pontificate fought for the Fifth Council in the West. It repaired church property wrecked by the Greek-Gothic wars. He refurnished churches and set church revenues in order for the poor. He died on 3 March 561.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-eu:
Eugene I was elected on 10 August 654 and died at Rome on 2 June 657. He took over after Martin I was dragged from Rome by Byzantine power for refusing dictation on Monothelitism. Martin died in exile in September 655. For a time Rome was governed by the archpriest, archdeacon, and chief notary. Eugene, a Roman cleric from his earliest years, was praised for gentleness, sanctity, and generosity.

Whether the emperor forced him onto the chair or Martin's supporters chose him against Martin's will, the imperial gamble failed. Martin later accepted his election. Eugene's first act was to send legates to Constantinople with his profession of faith. His legates were deceived or won over, returning with a synodical letter from Patriarch Peter. The entry follows the tangle of his short reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-ju:
Julius I was elected pope on 6 February 337, after a four-month vacancy. He was a Roman, son of Rusticus. His pontificate is famed for firm, judicious action in the Arian controversies. After Constantine the Great died, Constantine II let the exiled Athanasius return to Alexandria. Egyptian Arians set up the rival Pistus and asked Julius to admit him.

Athanasius sent his own envoys with a synodal letter justifying him. The Arian envoys begged Julius to call a great synod, and he summoned one at Rome, inviting the Eastern bishops. He insisted that the Alexandrian church should have written to Rome first, so that justice could be defined from there. With Constans's backing he helped bring about the Council of Sardica in 342 or 343, sending Archidamus, Philoxenus, and Leo as his men. The Eastern Arian bishops refused to join and left.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-lu:
Lucius I reigned from 253 to 254 and died at Rome on 5 March 254. After Cornelius's summer 253 death in exile, Lucius won choice and consecration as Rome's bishop. Nothing is known of his early life. The Liber Pontificalis calls him Roman-born, son of Porphyrius, though its source is unknown. Gallus's persecution still raged, and Lucius was soon exiled too.

He was allowed back, presumably when Valerian became emperor. Cyprian wrote twice to congratulate him, first on his elevation and exile, then on his return with his companions. Lucius followed Cornelius and Cyprian on the Lapsi, the fallen: those who had done penance should not be denied communion and peace. One calendar dates his death 5 March, another 4 March.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-ma:
Martin I's birthplace was Todi on the Tiber; Fabricius was his father. He was elected at Rome on 21 July 649 to succeed Theodore I. His biographer calls him nobly born, a great student of commanding intelligence, profound learning, and great charity to the poor. He governed when Monothelite leaders, backed by the emperor, strove to spread their tenets east and west. Theodore had sent him to Constantinople to arrange the deposition of the heretical patriarch Pyrrhus.

Martin had himself consecrated without waiting for imperial confirmation. He soon called a Lateran council of one hundred and five bishops. Exarch Olympius tried to build a faction for the emperor and then to kill the pope at communion, but failed and left for Sicily. Constans then sent Calliopas, who entered the Lateran on 17 June 653, declared Martin deposed, and ordered him to Constantinople. Martin forbade resistance to avoid bloodshed. He died at Cherson on 16 September 655.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-ni:
Nicholas I was born at Rome, son of the Defensor Theodore. Sergius II made him subdeacon and Leo IV made him deacon. After Benedict died in April 858, Emperor Louis II came to Rome to sway the election. Nicholas was elected on 24 April and consecrated and enthroned the same day in St Peter's.

Western Christendom was in a sorry state: Charlemagne's empire had splintered, bishops were worldly, and morality was despised. Nicholas stood as a conscientious voice of the Roman primacy, defending Christian marriage and discipline. He ordered bishops under Charles the Bold to excommunicate Ingiltrud unless she returned to her husband Boso. He fought Lothair II of Lorraine over his abandonment of his lawful wife Theutberga for Waldrada. When Lorraine's bishops approved the illicit union at Aachen in 862 and bribed legates assented at Metz in 863, he brought the case to his own tribunal. He died on 13 November 867.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-agape:
Agapetus I reigned from 535 to 536 and died on 22 April 536. Gordianus, a Roman priest killed in riots under Symmachus, was his father. His first act was to burn, before the assembled clergy, Boniface II's anathema against his rival Dioscurus. He confirmed Carthage's decrees barring Arian converts from orders. He gave Contumeliosus of Riez a new trial before papal delegates.

Gothic king Theodehad begged the aged pope to plead with Justinian at Constantinople against Belisarius's invasion. Agapetus pledged the church's sacred vessels to pay for the journey and sailed in midwinter with five bishops. Justinian would not abandon Italy, but the visit triumphed ecclesiastically. The patriarch Anthimus, an intruder backed by Theodora, refused to profess faith and return to Trebizond, so Agapetus broke with him. The entry closes with his death on 22 April 536.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-alexa:
Alexander I is reckoned by Irenaeus as the fifth pope after the apostles. Critics date his pontificate around 106 to 115 or 109 to 116. Christian antiquity credits him with about ten years, and he stands on the Roman bishops' list drawn up by Hegesippus before 189. A fifth-century Roman tradition says he was Roman-born, ruled under Trajan, and died a martyr by beheading on the Via Nomentana on 3 May.

Tradition also credits him, scarcely with accuracy, with adding the Qui Pridie words on the Eucharist to the canon. He is said to have introduced blessed water mixed with salt for cleansing Christian homes. That early Roman custom lives on in the Gelasian Sacramentary's blessing, close to the Asperges prayer at Mass's start. In 1855 a cemetery of Alexander, Eventulus, and Theodulus was found near Rome at the traditional spot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-anast: Anastasius I is remembered chiefly for condemning Origenism. Roman born, he took the papal office in 399 and died under four years later. Augustine, Jerome, and Paulinus were among his friends. Jerome calls him a man of great holiness, rich in his poverty. He reigned during the barbarian invasions. His stand against Origenism marks his reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-bonif:
Boniface I was elected on 28 December 418 and died at Rome on 4 September 422. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Roman, son of Jocundus the presbyter. Damasus I is believed to have ordained him, and he is believed to have represented Innocent I at Constantinople around 405. Little else is known before his election.

After Zosimus died, deacons seized the Lateran and elected Archdeacon Eulalius. The higher clergy met next day at St Theodora's church and chose the aged Boniface against his will. Both entered office on 29 December, and Rome fell into tumult. The prefect Symmachus backed Eulalius and won the emperor's backing, and Boniface was expelled. Boniface later trimmed Arles's leading rights, restoring province bishops, and handled Africa's appeals, including the case of Apiarius, raised by Carthage in May 419.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-celes:
Celestine I was a Roman, son of Priscus. He is said to have lived at Milan with Ambrose. The first firm notice of him comes in Innocent I's document of 416, calling him Celestine the Deacon. Augustine wrote to him reverently in 418. He succeeded Boniface I on 10 September 422 and died on 26 July 432, after nine years, ten months, and sixteen days.

He was elected without opposition despite stormy times. After Augustine died in 430, Celestine praised his sanctity, learning, and zeal to Gaul's bishops and barred Semipelagian attacks on his memory. Manichaeans, Donatists, Novatians, and Pelagians troubled the church while barbarians pressed the empire, yet his firm, gentle character met each crisis. His last years were consumed by the Nestorian struggle in the East. He had Cyril of Alexandria investigate Nestorius, condemned his errors at a Roman synod in 430, and ordered Cyril to proceed against him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-cleme:
Clement I, called Clemens Romanus, is the first successor of Peter about whom anything definite is known. He stands first among the Apostolic Fathers, and his feast falls on 23 November. One genuine writing survives from him, a letter to the Church of Corinth, while many others bear his name falsely. Tertullian says Rome claimed Peter ordained him. Jerome notes most Latins made him Peter's immediate successor, though he himself rightly calls Clement the fourth pope.

The oldest pope list, made by Hegesippus around 160, passed through Irenaeus, Africanus, and Hippolytus into the Liberian Catalogue and the Liber Pontificalis. Eusebius used Africanus with slight date corrections, and Jerome's chronicle translates Eusebius. The entry then turns to Clement's Corinthian letter, urging repentance, unity, and peace on a divided church. It closes with a Eucharistic prayer and a blessing on every soul called by God's holy name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-damas:
Damasus I was born about 304 and died on 11 December 384. His father Antonius was probably Spanish, and he grew up serving St Laurence's church at Rome. He was elected in October 366 by a large majority. Supporters of the late Liberius rejected him, chose Deacon Ursinus, and used violence to seat their man. Valentinian backed Damasus and exiled Ursinus to Cologne in 367.

Ursinus's party kept persecuting him, and an adultery charge in 378 failed before Gratian and a synod of forty-four bishops, which excommunicated his accusers. Damasus condemned Apollinarianism and Macedonianism at Roman synods in 368 and 369. He lived to welcome Theodosius's edict of 380 making Peter's faith the state's religion. He secured Rome's authority in Illyricum through a vicar at Thessalonica. He grounded Rome's supremacy not on councils but on Christ's words to Peter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-felix:
Felix I died in 274. Early in 269 he followed Dionysius at the Roman church's head. About then Rome received Antioch's report that its synod had deposed Paul of Samosata for heretical teaching on the Trinity. Felix probably answered the East with a letter expounding Trinitarian doctrine. An Apollinarist follower later interpolated that letter for his sect. The doctored text reached the Council of Ephesus in 431.

The surviving fragment stresses Christ's single unity as both Son of God and Son of Man. It also calls Felix a martyr, but no authentic early evidence supports that, and the detail likely comes from confusing names. The Liber Pontificalis says Felix built a basilica on the Via Aurelia and was buried there. That burial detail is evidently wrong: the fourth-century calendar places his burial in the Callistus Catacomb on the Via Appia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-gelas:
Gelasius I died at Rome on 19 November 496. He called himself Roman-born, though the Liber Pontificalis calls him African, a phrase some read as African origin and others as Roman citizenship. Before his election on 1 March 492, his predecessor Felix employed him heavily in drafting church documents, so heavily that scholars sometimes confuse the two men's writings.

Gelasius showed firmness at once against Acacius's adherents. Neither Euphemius of Constantinople nor Emperor Anastasius could win recognition on terms that compromised Peter's chair. He defended Alexandria and Antioch as second and third sees and refused to let a city's temporal rank set its church rank. He set ordinations on ember days and enforced a fourfold split of church revenues: for the poor, for churches and worship, for the bishop, and for the minor clergy. Manichaeans hiding in Rome betrayed themselves by refusing the chalice, since they held wine impure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-john-:
John I was a Tuscan, son of Constantius. After a seven-day interregnum he was elected on 13 August 523 and held the see two years, nine months, and seven days. He died at Ravenna on 18 or 19 May 526. Nothing is known of his administration: his Bullarium holds only two letters, both almost certainly apocryphal.

We know only his journey to Constantinople, vaguely, though it mattered greatly and caused his death. Emperor Justin's 523 decree against Arians forced them to hand churches to Catholics. Theodoric, the Ostrogoth king and Arian champion, resented the blow and feared Roman senators dealing secretly with Byzantium. Early in 525 he sent an embassy of senators to the emperor, forcing the pope to lead it and seek withdrawal of the edict. The entry follows the mission that ended in John's death at Ravenna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-marce:
Marcellus I was elected pope in May or June 308 and died in 309. After Marcellinus died in 304, persecution raged on, and even after Diocletian abdicated in 305 and Maxentius took Rome in 306, a new bishop's choice waited nearly two years. At Rome Marcellus found the church in great confusion. Meeting places and burial grounds had been confiscated, and ordinary church life was broken.

Worse, many who had lapsed under persecution now violently demanded readmission without penance. The Liber Pontificalis says Marcellus split Rome's church administration into twenty-five districts, or tituli, each under a presbyter. Those priests prepared catechumens for baptism and led their districts' life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-pius-:
Pius I was pope from about 140 to about 154. Irenaeus's earliest pope list makes him the ninth successor of Peter. The Liberian list's dates of 146 to 161 rest on false calculation and cannot stand. The one firm chronological peg is Polycarp's death in 155 or 156: visiting Rome the year before, Polycarp found Anicetus, Pius's successor, already bishop there. Pius must therefore have died about 154.

The Liber Pontificalis names Rufinus as his father and Aquileia as his birthplace, probably a guess from the later Rufinus of Aquileia. The Liberian list, confirmed by the Muratorian Fragment, says his brother Hermas published The Shepherd. Hermas's tale of himself, first slave then freedman, may be fiction. During Pius's reign heretics visited Rome to spread false doctrine, among them the Gnostic Valentinus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-sergi:
Sergius I reigned from 687 to 701 and was probably consecrated on 15 December 687. As Conon lay dying, Archdeacon Pascal bribed the exarch for the succession, while another faction chose Archpriest Theodore. Clergy and people set both aside and chose Sergius instead. He was an Antioch native, son of Tiberius, schooled in Sicily and ordained by Leo II.

He kept close ties with England. He received Caedwalla, king of the West Saxons, baptized him in 689, and buried him in St Peter's when he died at Rome. He restored Wilfrid to his see, favoured Aldhelm of Malmesbury, and consecrated Willibrord bishop to preach to the Frisians. When Justinian demanded he sign the Quinisext Council of 692, which let married clergy keep wives and raised Constantinople level with Rome, Sergius refused. The emperor sent an officer to seize him, but the people shielded him, and Justinian was soon deposed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-sixtu:
Sixtus I, spelled Xystus in the oldest documents, succeeded Alexander and was followed by Telesphorus. The Liberian list places his reign under Hadrian, from 117 to 126. Eusebius's Chronicon gives 114 to 124, while his History gives 114 to 128. All authorities agree he reigned about ten years. He was Roman-born, son of Pastor.

The Liber Pontificalis credits him with three ordinances. Only sacred ministers may touch sacred vessels. Bishops summoned to Rome must present apostolic letters on returning home. After the Preface the priest recites the Sanctus with the people. The Felician list and martyrologies call him a martyr. His feast falls on 6 April. His grave lies in the Vatican beside Peter's tomb. His relics are said to have moved to Alatri in 1132, though one scholar contends they remain in the Vatican.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-steph:
Stephen I was probably consecrated on 12 May 254 and died on 2 August 257, though his dates are uncertain. Ancient lists call him a Roman, son of Jovius. The Liber Pontificalis says Lucius I, facing martyrdom, left the church's care with his archdeacon Stephen. Stephen's known story mostly touches the heretic Novatus.

His great work was defending heretical baptism's validity against Cyprian and bishops of Africa and Asia. That controversy's history belongs under Baptism and Cyprian, but newly found letters of Dionysius of Alexandria bear on it. Benson judged that Stephen triumphed, and Rome with him, as deserved. Early in his reign Faustinus of Lyons urged him against Marcian of Arles, who followed Novatus and denied communion to penitent lapsi. Stephen did not move, so Gaul's bishops asked Cyprian to write to the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-victo:
Victor I reigned from 189 to 198 or 199, though his birth date is unknown. The Liber Pontificalis calls him an African, son of Felix. The Liberian list gives 186 to 197, while Eusebius differs on his dates. Under Commodus and early Septimius Severus, Rome's church generally enjoyed external peace.

Commodus's favour toward Christians is credited to Marcia. She summoned Victor to the palace and asked for a list of Christians condemned to Sardinia's mines. Victor gave it, and Marcia won their pardon from the emperor. Hyacinthus carried the release to Sardinia. Later Victor pressed Asia's bishops to keep Easter always on Sunday, threatening exclusion from fellowship. Irenaeus and others blamed his severity and urged peace, noting his predecessors had kept Sunday without breaking friendship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sylveste:
Sylvester I died on 31 December 335. The Liber Pontificalis calls him son of the Roman Rufinus, while the legendary Life of Sylvester names his mother Justa. After Miltiades died, Sylvester became Rome's bishop for twenty-one years. His reign fell in Constantine the Great's era, when the church's public standing improved greatly, yet authoritative information about his pontificate is regrettably thin.

Legend soon tied him to Constantine in ways contrary to fact. Tales of his persecution, of healing and baptizing the emperor, of imperial gifts and rights, and of a 275-bishop Roman council are entirely legendary. They spread through the Life, the apocryphal Constitutum Sylvestri, and the Donation of Constantine. What stands is his part in the Arian negotiations and Nicaea: the word homoousion was probably agreed with him beforehand, and he sent legates to the first ecumenical council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-theodore:
Theodore I was pope from 642 to 649, though his birth date is unknown. A Greek of Jerusalem, son of Bishop Theodore, he won prompt confirmation from Ravenna's exarch, perhaps because he was Greek, and was consecrated on 24 November 642. His whole reign fought Monothelitism.

At once he told Constans II he could not recognize Paul as Constantinople's patriarch, since Pyrrhus's deposition had not been canonical, and urged withdrawal of the Ecthesis. He pressed Paul and his consecrators on Pyrrhus's legal deposition. Cyprus, Palestine, and Africa submitted loyally to his teaching. Pyrrhus recanted before him in 645 but relapsed and was excommunicated in 648. At Africa's bishops' urging, Theodore tried again to reclaim Paul, who declared for one Will in Christ, and Rome sentenced him to excommunication and deposition in 649. Paul answered by mistreating papal nuncios and winning the Typus decree from Constans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-urban-i:
Urban I reigned from 222 to 230 and died on 23 May 230. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Roman, son of Pontianus. After Callistus I died on 14 October 222, Urban was elected Rome's bishop, heading the church eight years. Hippolytus's schism continued through his reign, and Hippolytus probably wrote his Philosophumena attacking Callistus during it.

Urban kept his predecessor's line toward the schismatics. Alexander Severus became emperor in 222, favouring religious eclecticism and protecting Christians. Lampridius stresses that Alexander made no trouble for Christians. Rome's church therefore enjoyed essential peace, though its legal status stayed unchanged. Claims that he converted many rest on Cecilia's Acts, and the silver-vessel tale is a later editor's invention. He probably died naturally, judging from the era's peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gennadius-:
Gennadius I, patriarch of Constantinople from 458 to 471, left scarcely any writings, yet his council's letter against simony survives. Facundus reports he wrote against Cyril of Alexandria about 431, more violently even than Ibas's letter, though Cyril's letter of 434 may show them friends by then. Succeeding Anatolius in 458, he received Leo's warning of 17 June 460 against Timothy Aelurus, Monophysite intruder at Alexandria. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows a patriarch known through others' letters.

Not later than 459 he gathered a council of eighty-one bishops, many from the East and Egypt, including men dispossessed by Aelurus. Its letter against simony, the buying of church office, is preserved in Mansi's collection. About the same time Daniel the Stylite mounted his column near the city, apparently without patriarchal leave. The entry sketches authority exercised through council and correspondence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-germanus-i:
Germanus I, patriarch of Constantinople from 715 to 730, lost his see for refusing an emperor's ban on images. Born at Constantinople late in Heraclius's reign to the noble Justinianus, he served at the cathedral, then became bishop of Cyzicus. At the synod of 712 he bowed with most Greek bishops to the emperor's new doctrine. True doctrine returned under Anastasius II. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 733 or 740.

As patriarch he defended the honour given to images in letters to Thomas of Claudiopolis and in debate with Constantine, whom he seemingly won over. Leo III pressed on, reading a volcanic eruption as judgment on idol worship and issuing his edict of 726. Germanus opposed him, won Gregory II's praise in 729, and in 730 refused to sign the imperial ban before a council. Forced to resign, he yielded to the pliant Anastasius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodosius-i:
Emperor Theodosius I, whom all call Great, ruled Rome's East with faith and iron will. Born in Spain about 346, he died at Milan on 17 January 395. He stamped out the last traces of pagan worship, ended Arian heresy in the empire, made peace with the Goths, and gave a famous show of penance for a crime. His father, General Comes Theodosius, and mother Thermantia were Catholics when Arianism stood at its height.

The son served well in the army, led Moesia as Dux, and beat the Sarmatians. His father's fall and death in 376 sent him home to Spain in disgrace. Gratian, after Valens died in 378, lifted him to fellow-emperor for the East on 19 January 379. Wed to Aelia Flacilla, father of Arcadius and Honorius, he ruled with law, faith, and a penitent heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valentinian-i:
Valentinian I, Flavius Valentinianus, ruled the West as emperor from 364 to 375. Born at Cibalis in Pannonia in 321 to humble parents, he entered the army young and became tribune of the scutarii about 360. He marched with Julian the Apostate to Antioch and was exiled to Gaul for refusing to honour idols. On Jovian's death he was proclaimed emperor on 26 February 364 and at once named his brother Valens ruler of the East.

He campaigned in Gaul against Alamanni and Burgundians, beating them at Châlons-sur-Marne, losing Mainz to them in 367, and overthrowing them at Solicinium at heavy cost. In 374 he made a treaty with their king Macrianus. The entry follows his reign, his religious tolerance, and his death at Bregetio near Pressburg on 17 November 375, during an audience with Quadi envoys.
cetywayo-and-his-white-neighbours-remark:
H. Rider Haggard first published his remarks on South Africa in 1882, three years after the Zulu war. He opens with speeches by Sir Garnet Wolseley and Lord Kimberley insisting Britain would never hand the Transvaal back. Against that fixed point he sets the history of Cetywayo, king of the Zulus, and the settlement imposed after his defeat.

Chaka, Dingaan, and Panda lead into Cetywayo's coronation, his army, and the war's causes. Haggard attacks Wolseley's settlement hard: carelessly chosen chiefs, fresh slaughter in Zululand, and a disappointed people. Natal colonists, Boer intentions, and the annexation of the Transvaal all come under review. The book argues policy from close knowledge of the ground.
chambers-s-elementary-science-readers-bo:
W. and R. Chambers built their Elementary Science Readers for the youngest schoolchildren, and Book I teaches by object lessons, each reading paired with a short lesson summary at the back. The cat comes first, in large simple words with accents marked: a child watches a cat wash, stretch, and slide out its claws from their sheaths.

Lessons move through the dog, buttercups and daisies, wheat, slate, and chalk, then on to the mouse, rabbit, ivy, bricks, and the donkey. Coffee, paper, the fly and wasp, the sunflower and rose all earn a page. Wood, coal, and fire end the course. Every common thing near a child's home becomes a first fact about the world.
collected-poems-1901-1918-in-two-volumes:
Collected Poems 1901–1918 in Two Volumes, Volume I, by Walter de la Mare, opens with the poems of The Listeners, 1914. A death-dream group leads, with Napoleon, England, and Truce among its titles. Characters from Shakespeare follow as short portraits: Falstaff, Macbeth, Iago, Ophelia, and Hamlet each get a poem.

Sonnets and Memories of Childhood fill the middle of the volume. The poems under the book's own title include Old Susan, Miss Loo, Arabia, The Dark Château, and The Listeners itself. A second gathering, Motley, 1918, closes the volume. Its titles turn stranger: The Little Salamander, The Sunken Garden, The Blind Boy, The Empty House, and The Revenant.
doe-osti-2574952-methodopt-a-shiny-based:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2024-00414, by Benjamin Luke and Stephanie Gamble in May 2025, introduces MethodOpt, a point-and-click tool for tuning lab instruments. Tools such as gas chromatograph mass spectrometers have many settings at once, and the best mix is found by trial. The usual one-setting-at-a-time approach is slow and misses how settings interact.

MethodOpt wraps a modern search method, one that tunes many settings toward several goals at once, in a Shiny web interface. Users lay out fractional factorial test plans, run variance analysis, and plot trade-offs without writing code. The approach saves substantial time and resources compared with older method development, the authors report. The tool was built under the laboratory's internal LDRD research program.
doe-osti-2584405-a-novel-sediment-passag:
Final technical report for award DE-EE0008947, from the University of Minnesota's St. Anthony Falls Laboratory under Jeffrey Marr, designs a passage for the river's own cargo: sediment. Dams trap sand that downstream reaches starve for, while reservoirs fill with the surplus. The project, February 2020 to September 2024, advanced a modular sediment bypass for new low-head hydropower, meant to keep sediment moving past the dam at something like its natural rate.

The team reviewed sand bed rivers and chose example sites, then iterated the module design across two budget periods with a go/no-go review between them. Readiness rose from TRL 2 to TRL 3 or 4. Partners included Barr Engineering, Utah State's Peter Wilcock, and Voigt Consultants. Design goals were threefold: stop reservoirs silting up, restore continuity of sediment transport, and prevent the scouring or buildup that unnatural sediment patterns cause downstream. The report archives how the design changed and why.
doe-osti-2587594-artificial-intelligence:
Dated August 10, 2025, this final scientific report closes Department of Energy award DE-EE0009212. The project applied artificial intelligence to transit agencies that run mixed fleets, with a focus on paratransit: the demand-response service that carries riders who book trips in advance or on the day. Scheduling those trips well is a hard problem that changes hour by hour.

The report tracks three phases. Algorithms cover an offline vehicle routing problem that knows some bookings ahead, a rolling horizon scheduler, and an online scheduling method for requests that arrive live. A simulation environment called Transit-Gym, extended as E-Transit Bench with electric grid simulation, let the team test ideas safely. Other threads improved rider occupancy estimation with neural networks and computer vision, built a paratransit web application, and engaged the community. Later chapters prepare a field test and review go/no-go milestones.
doe-osti-2588428-technologies-for-enhanc:
Matthew Searle, Owen Grabowski, and Douglas Straub of the National Energy Technology Laboratory wrote this technology review, DOE/NETL-2025/4938, dated July 9, 2025. Its subject is condensation inside supercritical carbon dioxide power cycles. How well the cooler condenses CO2 near its critical point strongly moves plant efficiency and the levelized cost of electricity, so better condenser surfaces pay off across the whole cycle.

The review surveys passive heat transfer enhancement: surfaces that boost condensation without moving parts. Established designs include helical micro-ribs inside tubes, documented in earlier literature. Newer options use additive manufacturing, such as conical pin arrays printed as part of the heat exchanger. Screening analysis and benchmark correlations compare the candidates, treating both stratified and annular two-phase flow regimes. The report closes with a recommended concept for enhanced condensation hardware in direct-fired sCO2 cycles.
doe-osti-2997304-exploring-transport-ena:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-12246, by Craig Hogle, Evan Johnson, Jonathan Sterk, Tharon Morrison, and Dan Stick, dated September 2025, works toward a scalable trapped-ion quantum computer. Ions held in traps serve as qubits, and light pulses steer them. The project combines two scaling ideas: shuttling ions between zones to run gates, and addressing them with light guides built into the chip.

Hardware chapters detail the pulse gear that times the shuttling. A simple pulser board fires trigger pulses to a digital-to-analog chassis when a move begins, without tracking the waveform details itself. Prior team results cited include high-fidelity ion operations with photonic modulators and multi-site optical addressing of trapped ions. The report assembles the control stack a larger ion machine will need.
doe-osti-2997654-simulations-of-radiatio:
University of Michigan final report on award DE-SC0023699, led by Carolyn Kuranz, covers simulation work from April 2023 to March 2025 on radiation flow in strongly coupled plasmas. In such plasmas the electric energy between ions beats their thermal energy, changing how radiation is absorbed and emitted. The physics runs from stellar interiors to shocks at the edges of forming galaxies.

The team built a ray-tracing program that follows radiation through a simulated neutron star capsule implosion, under conditions matched to Omega-60 laser experiments. The capsule was modeled in two dimensions as concentric rings of plastic, nickel, and helium, each with its own absorption and emission traits. Ray paths through the rings were derived on paper, then coded, and the rays were summed into the signal a distant detector would see. The short filing states the method and its target experiment.
doe-osti-2999078-isotopics-by-nuclides-t:
William Johnson of Sandia National Laboratories tests a gamma-spectrum analysis tool in report SAND2025-12717, printed September 2025. The tool, called Isotopics by Nuclides, sits inside InterSpec, a free program for reading radiation spectra. From a spectrum it estimates how much of each isotope a sample holds, the sort of answer inspectors need for uranium and plutonium checks.

Test cases used real measurements from an H3D M400 detector, a portable cadmium zinc telluride instrument. Uranium and plutonium runs were checked first, then a mixed sample of highly enriched and low enriched uranium. A harder case was simulated: a solid sphere of 90 percent enriched uranium wrapped in depleted uranium, generated with the GADRAS code. One tuned setting, shipped as a preset, handled each family of spectra. The report records where the tool reads enrichment well and where shielding or mixing strains it.
doe-osti-3000610-implementation-of-a-tur:
Chris Chartrand of Sandia National Laboratories reports a laboratory-directed project in SAND2025-13481R, printed September 2025, that puts wind farms inside a global climate model. Wind farms have spread widely, yet their full effect on Earth systems is poorly known. Each turbine steals momentum from the wind and stirs turbulence behind it, and thousands together might nudge rain, soil moisture or even the jet stream.

The project implemented a turbine farm model in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, the big coupled simulator that joins atmosphere, ocean and land chemistry. The new module extracts momentum from the modelled airflow wherever farms stand. With it, scientists can run decades-long simulations and watch precipitation, extreme weather, soil moisture and jet stream position respond. The tool is meant to inform where farms get built, weighing clean energy gains against real effects on the natural systems around them.
doe-osti-3006948-integrating-cyber-infor:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/CON-25-88262, by Benjamin Lampe and Russell Gold and dated September 30, 2025, explains how cyber-informed engineering fits into process automation. The approach starts from the physical harm an attack could cause, then designs the control system so that harm cannot happen. Programmable logic controllers, the small computers that run plant equipment, get close attention throughout.

Working through the CIE principles one by one, the authors show how engineers can add system-wide protections. They question digital features the plant does not need and keep manual or physical fallbacks in place. The method is also tied to federal risk rules that plants must meet to win an authorization to operate. Plant engineers get a practical route to safer automated systems.
doe-osti-3011876-a-comprehensive-study-o:
Inverter based units change how protection relays behave. Jing Wang and Andy Hoke of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, with University of Idaho coauthors, tested generic inverter models and control choices against relay elements used on transmission systems. Both grid following and grid forming style controls enter the analysis. Relay elements are the parts of a protection relay that sense faults and trip breakers.

Time domain elements get a close look. The incremental quantity distance element TD21 needs its operating signal to exceed the restraining signal, of opposite sign. The directional element TD32 guards permissive overreaching transfer trip schemes. The November 2025 report works element by element through the consequences.
doe-osti-3013245-guidance-for-grid-resil:
NREL authors Reiko Matsuda-Dunn, Jordan Burns, Abodh Poudyal, and five colleagues wrote this November 2025 guidance on grid resilience decisions for rural Minnesota. Rural electric cooperatives run long distribution lines through storm country with small staffs and tight budgets. The report identifies which weather hazards hit Minnesota distribution systems hardest and how utilities currently choose resilience investments.

Outage and grid data came from seven participating electric cooperatives. The analysis links wind-related outages to line and pole attributes and reviews the metrics utilities use, or lack, in planning. A long section catalogs which customers depend most on power, from people on medical devices to shelters and public safety sites. The guidance aims to help small utilities defend resilience spending with evidence.
doe-osti-3013781-num-dat-file-format-spe:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-20193, by John Lang Jr., William Anderson, Frank Cherne, Rachel Huber, and Michael Hargather, issued January 12, 2026, specifies the NUM-DAT file format used to archive data from the M-9 gun experiments. M-9 is Los Alamos's Shock and Detonation Physics group, which fires gas guns to study how materials behave under extreme pressure. Consistent archiving keeps decades of shot data readable.

The specification defines the structure of the group's .num and .dat files so any analyst can parse them the same way. A comparison table places the format beside alternatives the group encounters: Nevada Test Site .dig files, comma-separated text, Tektronix oscilloscope waveforms, and MATLAB files. Worked example data and a MATLAB reader in the appendix let new staff validate their own tools.
doe-osti-3015015-toward-automated-plasma: Automated calibration of a plasma focused ion beam instrument is the subject of a July 24, 2025 SULI poster by Emerson Liu with Hoffmann, Gannon, and Spurgeon. Computer vision scores spot burns cut into silicon, giving figures of merit for astigmatism, quad, and focus. A UNet++ model segments the burns from microscope images, reaching a stig score of 0.9128 on the example shown. As a single-page poster, it gives the approach and early results rather than a full study; future work adds focus and quad scores and more training data.
doe-osti-3015064-the-manufacture-of-adva:
NLR/TP-6A50-96472, dated January 2026, is the MAKE IT Prize final technical report. Holly and Sweet wrote it. Domestic energy manufacturing is its subject. The prize paid teams to plan and ready factories for key energy systems inside the United States.

Two tracks ran in parallel. Facilities Track winners first produced a sound plan for a plant. They then proved themselves shovel-ready. Site control, permits, financing, and community backing were all in hand. The Strategies Track rewarded new manufacturing joint ventures across regions. Winners ranged from Beatrice, Nebraska to Pittsfield, Massachusetts and Riverside, California. Support came through Power Connectors in the American-Made network. They ran peer exchanges, matchmaking webinars, and expert sessions free to competitors.
doe-osti-3015716-assembly-and-repair-of-:
Louisiana State University's final technical report for award DE-SC0020119 covers a project led by David J Vinyard from September 2019 to August 2024. The subject is Photosystem II, the protein complex that uses sunlight to split water in plants and related organisms. The team studied how this complex is built, and how damaged copies get taken apart and repaired.

Work ran along three lines: protein contacts that help assembly, the chemistry that builds the manganese-calcium oxygen-evolving complex, and the steps that mark worn centers for breakdown. Methods included electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, protein chemistry, genetics, mass spectrometry, and computer modeling. Results show that proton release limits early assembly steps, while chloride and calcium ions help manganese oxidation. The findings matter for anyone designing artificial photosynthesis systems.
doe-osti-3017119-transitions-dynamics-an:
Thomas F Rosenbaum of the California Institute of Technology wrote this revised final report for award DE-SC0014866. The project studied transitions, dynamics, and driven states in quantum magnets. Its test system was a physical version of the transverse-field Ising model, a standard model of magnetism where a sideways magnetic field acts as a quantum tuning knob.

The team probed collective electronuclear modes at a quantum phase transition in pure and disordered ferromagnets. They traced behavior from single spin flips to whole domain tunneling in a ferromagnet driven around its hysteresis loop. Quantum and classical annealing runs were compared through their fluctuation spectra. Tools included ac and dc magnetometry, Barkhausen noise measurement, and microwave studies. The work speaks to basic questions about stability, coherence, and control in quantum materials, with an eye on future quantum devices.
doe-osti-3019572-m3as-25in1002073-analys:
Timothy Le Phero, Bibo Zhong, Michael D McMurtrey, and five colleagues at Idaho National Laboratory analyzed irradiated strain gauges in INL/RPT-25-89342, December 2025. The gauges were printed, not machined: silver nanoparticle ink on aluminum substrates, insulated with polyimide tape 25 micrometers thick. Printing promises conformal sensors for reactor internals. The question is whether they survive the environment they would measure. Irradiation testing ran at Ohio State's research reactor. Fixtures carried thermocouples to log temperature through the exposure.

The report's job is the data: what the gauges read under irradiation, and how far those readings can be trusted. Fabrication details, from ink choice to encapsulation, are documented so the results can be reproduced. Printed sensors that drift under neutron flux are curiosities; printed sensors with characterized drift are instruments. This analysis moves the gauges from the first class toward the second. Milestone M3AS-25IN1002073 is the deliverable the report closes.
doe-osti-3022719-equipment-assessment-gu:
INL guide INL/RPT-26-89297, from the Center for Securing Digital Energy Technology, gives power grid asset owners a step-by-step method. It covers inspecting and hardening the operational technology devices their systems depend on. Field devices and embedded systems are frequent cyber targets. Many owners have no structured way to check what is actually inside the boxes on their poles and in their substations.

The procedure walks through asset identification and verification, physical security and tamper inspection, firmware integrity checks, configuration baseline audits, port and communication security, and user account and access control.
